In coordination with the Department of the Interior and other Federal partners, BSEE advances the Trump Administration’s priority to unleash America’s offshore critical minerals and strategic resources, reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, and strengthen national security. The bureau provides scientific, technical, and regulatory expertise that helps ensure offshore operations are conducted in a manner that protects human life, safeguards marine and coastal environments, and conserves the Nation’s offshore resource for current and future generations.
The Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA) charges BSEE with promoting safety, environmental protection, and conservation of natural resources associated with offshore energy and mineral activities. Under OCSLA Section 1346, BSEE conducts research necessary to assess and manage activities associated with offshore oil, natural gas, and other mineral development, and this research is focused on improvements in safety, asset integrity, environmental protection, and efficient production. Section 1345 authorizes BSEE to enter into cooperative agreements with affected states for information sharing, joint use of expertise, and coordinated monitoring to carry out applicable Federal and State laws, regulations, and stipulations governing outer continental shelf operations, both offshore and onshore.

overview.objective:
To make funding available for water recycling projects. To develop and supplement urban and irrigation water supplies through water reuse—thereby improving efficiency, providing flexibility during water shortages, and diversifying water supply portfolios. Title XVI of P.L. 102-575, as amended (Title XVI), directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner, to undertake a program to identify and investigate opportunities to reclaim and reuse wastewaters and impaired ground and surface water in the 17 Western States and Hawaii. Title XVI provides authority for the Secretary to provide up to 25 percent of the cost of planning, design, and construction of water recycling projects, currently up to $40 million unless otherwise specified by Congress, as well as up to 50 percent of the cost of feasibility studies. Section 40905 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, P.L. 117-58 provides authority for the Secretary to provide up to 25 percent of the cost of planning, design, and construction of water recycling projects with a total estimate project cost of $500 million or more.

Title XVI of P.L. 102-575, as amended (Title XVI), directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner, to undertake a program to identify and investigate opportunities to reclaim and reuse wastewaters and impaired ground and surface water in the 17 Western States and Hawaii. Title XVI provides authority for the Secretary to provide up to 25 percent of the cost of planning, design, and construction of water recycling projects, currently up to $30 million unless otherwise specified by Congress, as well as up to 50 percent of the cost of feasibility studies.

The Water Desalination Act of 1996, as amended by P.L. 114-332 provides authority for the Secretary to provide up to 25 percent of the cost of planning, design, and construction of ocean or brackish water desalination facilities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Through the Water Recycling Programs, Reclamation provides cost-shared financial assistance on a competitive basis for planning, design, or construction of water recycling projects. Water recycling is an essential tool for stretching the limited water supplies in the Western United States.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to an entity to enhance an existing water reclamation facility’s infrastructure and treatment process to inject recycled water into a local aquifer for future extraction and use. The project will increase and protect the water supply to address drought impacts and provide an effluent disposal option to decrease environmental discharges to a local lake. Components of the project include design and construction of the advanced water purification facility, upgraded water treatment facilities, pump station improvements, wells, and conveyance pipelines to produce 2,000 acre-feet per year of potable water.

Reclamation provided funding to an entity to design and construct a project to produce purified recycled water by diverting tertiary effluent to a new advanced water purification facility that will use microfiltration, reverse osmosis, and an ultraviolet advanced oxidation process. The purified water will then be delivered to spreading grounds to replenish the groundwater basin. The project, once constructed, will reduce dependence on imported water by delivering 20,600 acre‐feet per year of recycled water, establishing a new local, and drought tolerant water supply.

overview.objective: Desalination and Water Purification Research (DWPR) Program aims to increase water supplies by reducing the costs, energy requirements, and other barriers to adoption of treating impaired water for beneficial uses. The DWPR Program works with Reclamation researchers and partners to develop innovative, cost-effective, and technologically efficient ways to desalinate and treat water. overview.objective: The objective of the WaterSMART Grants program is to leverage money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation for water management improvement projects, including: 1) water and energy efficiency grants that result in quantifiable water savings, increase water supply reliability, and implement hydropower; and 2) small-scale water efficiency projects that have been identified through previous planning efforts.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: WaterSMART Grants provide cost-shared financial assistance on a competitive basis to carry out projects focused on water conservation, hydropower, and small-scale water efficiency improvements.

list.description:
Reclamation’s Water and Energy Efficiency Grants provided funding to a water district in partnership with a ditch company and an irrigation district to replace 11 existing outdated manual headgates along two canals that divert irrigation water from the river with automated turnout gates coupled with a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system. The project also includes installation of two additional automated turnout gates to better control flow. The project is expected to result in annual water savings of 5,140 acre-feet, currently lost to leakage and over-delivery at the canal gates due to operational inefficiencies such as manual gate operation. Conserved water will remain in the river for recreational use, water supply, and other beneficial uses. 
Reclamation’s Small-Scale Water Efficiency Projects provided funding to a city to install 390 Advanced Metering Infrastructure meters, enabling the city to quickly identify and respond to water leaks and usage spikes; customers will have access to their water usage through an online portal. These improvements will help the city better manage its water supplies more efficiently and enhance the quality of its services. The project aligns with the goals of the state water development plan.

Reclamation’s Water and Energy Efficiency Grants provided funding to an irrigation district to improve existing irrigation infrastructure at nine sites across the district. The project will address problems such as canal seepage, inaccurate flow measurement, and loss from leakage by replacing gates, pipes, and outlet works. The project is expected to result in annual water savings of approximately 2,306 acre-feet, which will increase flows into two local reservoirs, reducing the need to divert water during the non-irrigation season to fill the reservoirs.
Reclamation’s Small-Scale Water Efficiency Projects provided funding to pipe 2,800 feet of irrigation canal to prevent seepage and enhance water conservation and conveyance. Piping the canal will prevent water loss from seepage and evaporation, allowing for more efficient management of water flow to match use demands and better conserve water for downstream irrigators.

title: Title II, Colorado River Basin Salinity Control

overview.objective: To provide financial and  technical assistance to: (1) identify salt source areas; (2) develop project plans to carry out conservation practices to reduce salt loads; (3) install conservation practices to reduce salinity levels; (4) carry out research, education, and demonstration activities; (5) carry out monitoring and devaluation activities; and (6) to decrease salt concentration and salt loading which causes increased salinity levels within the Colorado River and to enhance the supply and quality of water available for use.  Such programs shall consist of cost-effective measures and associated works to reduce salinity from saline springs, leaking wells, irrigation sources, industrial sources, erosion of public and private land, or other sources.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Colorado River Basin Salinity Control Program is a longstanding partnership led by Reclamation that works to reduce the amount of salt entering the Colorado River system, protecting water quality for millions of municipal, industrial, and agricultural users by improving off-farm systems like canal and ditch lining. It serves communities, farmers, local irrigation districts, and water users across all seven Basin States, offering funding, technical coordination, and project support under federal cost-share programs to help keep the river clean and productive. What makes the program unique is its basinwide collaboration among federal agencies, states, tribes, and hundreds of local partners, along with its proven success in removing more than 1.3 million tons of salt from the river system each year through practical, science-based solutions.

list.description: A project to provide salinity control improvements to a Canal. This project will install approximately 4,945 ft of pipe and 6,820 ft of shotcrete liner along the canal. It will also provide for headgate structure, gate replacement, and siphon installation; all with remote controls to allow the headgates to be operated remotely.

FY26: 	Three sections of canal will be lined with an impermeable membrane liner system and coated in shotcrete conforming to U.S. Bureau of Reclamation specifications. Old headgates within each section will be replaced with new concrete structures complete with trash screens and sacrificial anodes. The canal will be re-graded and shaped using a combination of imported materials and suitable on-site materials prior to installation of liner materials.

selectionCriteria.description:
In 1984, the Salinity Control Act was amended to direct the Secretary of the Interior to give preference to units which reduce salinity at the least cost per unit of salinity reduction (or cost-effectiveness).  Cost-effectiveness is defined as the Salinity Program’s annual cost per ton of salt prevented from entering the Colorado River system.  Conceptually, cost-effectiveness is analogous to determining the cost per mile to own and operate a car.  That computation combines the annual expenses (loan payments, gas, maintenance, etc.) and divides by the miles traveled each year.  The key to understanding this approach is to appreciate that the government evaluates all projects as if the money is borrowed from a loan institution and repaid in annual installments over the life of the project. This economic evaluation principle is required by the “Economic and Environmental Principles Guidelines for Water and Related Land Resources Implementation Studies,” March 1983.  This method lends consistency in the comparison of non-federally financed alternatives (which must borrow funds) to Federally financed projects.  

Each proposal will be evaluated by an application review committee in accordance with the following criteria and corresponding percentage weights: (a) Technical merit – those passing will be evaluated further; (b) Cost effectiveness – 35%, (the annual cost for each ton of salt load reduction, expressed in dollars per ton); (c) The ability to enable future on-farm projects with the USDA – 30%; (d) Performance risk factors– 25%. Detailed information will be included in each FOA or may be obtained from the Salinity Control Program contacts listed above.

awardProcedure.description: Reclamation will solicit proposals and award funding through a Notice of Funding Opportunity process.  The NOFO will request proposals from public and private sectors that would control salinity based on cost per ton.  The proposals will be ranked based on their cost effectiveness for preventing salt from entering the Colorado River system.  The ranking would consider risk factors that might affect the project's performance.  Upon receipt of applications/proposals by the date identified in the announcement(s), the applications will be reviewed to determine if application/proposal(s) are consistent with requirements identified in the announcements.  The application/proposal(s) are reviewed against identified criteria by a Federal technical team of experts, that may include representatives of states as advisors.  Based on the review, a ranking will be defined. Negotiations will be conducted and/or awards will be made based on recommendations from the technical experts.  Award will be based on those applications best meeting the needs of the program, including cost and risk factors.

overview.objective: Reclamation leverages Federal and non-Federal funding to work cooperatively with States, Tribes, and other entities as they plan for and implement actions to increase water supply and hydropower reliability. The WaterSMART Drought Response Program invites eligible applicants to submit proposals for projects designed to improve drought resilience by developing effective water management strategies and drought contingency plans. Funding under the Drought Response Program supports a range of initiatives including infrastructure improvements for increased water storage and distribution capabilities, water source diversification, decision-making tools for water management, and comprehensive planning to prepare for and respond to drought conditions.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Reclamation leverages Federal and non-Federal funding to work cooperatively with States, Tribes, and other entities as they plan for and implement actions to increase water supply and hydropower reliability. The WaterSMART Drought Response Program invites eligible applicants to submit proposals for projects designed to improve drought resilience by developing effective water management strategies and drought contingency plans. Funding under the Drought Response Program supports a range of initiatives including infrastructure improvements for increased water storage and distribution capabilities, water source diversification, decision-making tools for water management, and comprehensive planning to prepare for and respond to drought conditions.

list.description:
Reclamation provided funding to a water conservancy district to construct a water treatment plant with the capacity to treat up to 5 million gallons per day from local springs in a state that has experienced moderate to extreme drought conditions in seven of the past ten years.  During these drought periods, the district has become increasingly reliant on groundwater to meet demand.  Currently, the springs are not utilized for culinary water supply; therefore, developing this water source will enhance the district’s resilience to drought-driven water shortages, particularly in years of reduced surface water availability.  This project will augment existing groundwater capacity, providing a reliable source of water in drought years, while also offering greater operational flexibility for aquifer recovery during wetter years.  The project is a priority in the district's drought contingency plan, ensuring its alignment with long-term water management goals and preparedness strategies.

Reclamation provided funding to a county to construct three new groundwater wells and two observation wells to modernize a regional, multi-agency project, a key infrastructure protecting the aquifers from seawater intrusion. These aquifers supply drinking water to over 4 million residents and support regional water supply reliability. The county currently relies on three aging injection wells that will be decommissioned to prevent groundwater cross-contamination. Constructing new wells will allow the county to expand its available water supply and avoid interruption in service as the current wells are taken offline. The new injection wells will strengthen the barrier by forming a freshwater pressure ridge to block seawater inflow and will be capable of recharging up to 579 acre-feet per year.  This project supports sustainable water management by integrating the injection of advanced treated recycled water and helps to ensure the long-term reliability of water supplies for the region.

Reclamation provided funding to an irrigation district to reconstruct a siphon and canal system that serves more than 42,000 acres of irrigated lands. The district will build an approximately 2-mile-long canal and siphon system between a local lake and reservoir. The new siphon and canal to the reservoir will allow the district to capture and convey approximately 11,000 acre-feet per year of unused irrigation water from upstream irrigators and store an additional 13,500 acre-feet. The project is essential for irrigation, groundwater recharge, and fulfilling regional water management responsibilities under the river recovery implementation program and interstate compact.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding.  Program anticipates funding projects that increase water supply and hydropower reliability and develop effective water management strategies for long-term drought resiliency.

assistanceRestriction.description:
Any projects or project elements that are part of a water desalination or recycling project eligible for funding under Section 4009(a) or 4009(c) of the WIIN Act, P.L. 114-322 are not eligible for funding under this NOFO. In addition, if a water desalination, reclamation, or recycling project has a total estimated project cost of more than $20 million, that project is not eligible under this NOFO and should be pursued under the Title XVI Water Reclamation and Reuse Program or the WaterSMART Desalination Planning and Construction Program.

Funding of a small surface or groundwater storage project (including groundwater recharge, injection wells, and aquifer storage and recovery wells) with a total estimated project cost of more than $10 million, or that is a phase of a larger project that exceeds $10 million, is not eligible under this NOFO. Applicants proposing such projects may wish to consider Reclamation’s Small Storage Program.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The San Gabriel Basin Restoration Fund is a congressionally authorized and appropriated groundwater-cleanup funding mechanism for the San Gabriel Basin in Los Angeles County, California. The Fund is administered by the Secretary of the Interior through the Bureau of Reclamation in cooperation with authorized local entities, including the San Gabriel Basin Water Quality Authority (WQA). Federal assistance supports eligible design, construction, operation, and maintenance of water-quality projects addressing contaminated groundwater. The current WQA action is administered as a Project Grant. Funding is not awarded through an open Federal competition; annual funding is dependent on congressional appropriations and is administered under the statutory Restoration Fund authority.

title: Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins Endangered Fish Recovery
popularLongName: Upper Colorado and San Juan River Recovery Implementation Program

overview.objective: The Upper Colorado River and San Juan River Endangered Fish Recovery Programs (Recovery Programs) are partnerships composed of State, Tribal and Federal agencies, water and power interests, and environmental groups working to recover four endangered fish in the Upper Colorado and San Juan River basins while water development proceeds in accordance with federal and state laws and interstate compacts.  The Recovery Programs focus on seven elements of recovery: instream flow, habitat restoration, nonnative fish control, information and education, propagation and genetics, research and monitoring, and program management. To authorize the Bureau of Reclamation to provide cost sharing for the endangered fish recovery implementation programs for the Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The purpose of assistance listing 15.529 is to authorize the Bureau of Reclamation to provide cost sharing for the endangered fish recovery implementation programs for the Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins. The Recovery Programs are designed to help recover the Colorado pikeminnow, Razorback sucker, Bonytail, and Humpback chub while allowing water development to continue in the Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins.

list.description: In fiscal year 2025, the programs continued to implement management actions and projects to recover endangered fish in the areas of in-stream flow protection, habitat restoration, nonnative fish management, propagation and genetics, research and monitoring, information and education, and program management.  Specific examples include operations and maintenance of river flow gages and infrastructure, installation and maintenance of electronic fish monitoring systems, maintenance of online databases, coordination of reservoir operations for recovery of endangered fish, management of floodplain rearing habitats including stocking of endangered fish in managed wetlands, removal of nonnative fish, and propagation and stocking of endangered fish.

In fiscal year 2026, the programs continued to implement management actions and projects to recover endangered fish in the areas of in-stream flow protection, habitat restoration, non-native fish management, propagation, and genetics, research and monitoring, information and education, and program management. Specific examples include operations and maintenance of river flow gages and infrastructure, installation and maintenance of electronic fish monitoring systems, maintenance of online databases, coordination of reservoir operations for recovery of endangered fish, management of floodplain rearing habitats including stocking of endangered fish in managed wetlands, removal of nonnative fish, and propagation and stocking of endangered fish. In addition, a new project to examine the efficacy of prey training, creation of low velocity habitat for larval fish and accumulation of LiDAR data were completed.

In fiscal year 2027, many of the same projects will continue. In addition, two new projects to examine effects of removing non-native trees on improving habitat will be implemented as well as a project to better understand the response of native fishes to large influxes of sediment during flood events.

overview.objective: The goal of the Water Conservation Field Services Program (WCFSP) is to proactively encourage water conservation and water use efficiency in the operations of water projects. The WCFSP is designed to assist water users in water management planning and to make more efficient use of existing water supplies. The WCFSP is managed by each of Reclamation’s Regional Offices to address Reclamation-wide water conservation priorities and to meet local goals.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The WCFSP provides cost-shared funding to proactively encourage water conservation in water operations and to assist agricultural and urban water districts in preparing and implementing water conservation planning.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to a municipal water district for water conservation planning to best manage and conserve water in the Commercial, Industrial, & Institutional (CII) sector, a widely variable water use class that has historically been difficult to target. Retail water agencies and selected consultants will expand upon the first phase of the project to create new customized best management practices (BMP) implementation plans for at least six additional county retailers based on their specific needs and water conservation goals to increase water efficiency for CII water users. Additionally, CII customer accounts will also be classified in a standardized system. This allows water suppliers to best understand their CII customer base, what types of customers they serve and in what quantity, what sectors are top water users and identify top water users across various categories and is a key step to lay the groundwork for the BMP plans to be implemented effectively. The project will result in written water conservation and management plans that identify water conservation goals and the appropriate conservation measures and best management practices for the CII sector.

Reclamation provided funding to a community services district to implement its Synthetic Aperture Radar Leak Detection Program, a cutting-edge initiative designed to prove that small districts can leverage innovative technology to overcome budget constraints and achieve significant infrastructure improvements while cost-effectively develop a pro-active leak detection program at a lower cost than the water loss if left unaddressed.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Central Utah Project Completion Act (CUPCA) is contained within Titles II through VI of the Reclamation Projects Authorization and Adjustment Act of 1992 (Public Law 102-575).  Its purpose is to provide for the orderly completion of the Central Utah Project (CUP), which is the largest participating project of the 1956 Colorado River Storage Project (CRSP).  CUPCA does this by authorizing an increase in the appropriations ceiling for CUP, for which Titles III and IV specifically address fish, wildlife, and outdoor recreation mitigation and enhancement opportunities.  Title III, specifically Sections 314(c) and (d)1, authorizes mitigation actions to protect, restore and enhance wetland and upland ecosystems for the conservation of fish and wildlife resources in the Upper Colorado River Basin outside the State of Utah.

The Parties agree to work harmoniously to achieve the objectives of the project.  When disagreements arise between/among the Parties, they must be resolved according to the procedures discussed below:

1. The Parties shall attempt first to resolve disagreements through informal discussion among the subordinate staff.

2. If the disagreement cannot be resolved through informal discussion, each shall document the nature of the disagreement and bring it to the attention of their respective Project Officer.

3. After reviewing the facts of the disagreement, the Project Officers will arrange a formal meeting. The PARTIES will collectively decide on any varied approaches which might be used to resolve the disagreement. The PARTIES shall be responsible for their individual expenses related to any approach utilized to resolve the disagreement.

4. Ultimately, if all other attempts at resolving the disagreement fail, a decision will be made by the Department of the Interior whose decision shall be final and conclusive.

Any post award issue will be open for resolution in accordance with the above procedures, with the exception of continuation of the assistance agreement, or other matters specifically addressed by the agreement itself.

overview.objective: The MSCP’s purposes are: (1) Protect the lower Colorado River environment while ensuring the certainty of existing river water and power operations, (2) Address the needs of threatened and endangered wildlife under the Endangered Species Act, and (3) Reduce the likelihood of listing additional species along the lower Colorado River.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Lower Colorado River Multi Species Conservation Program (LCR MSCP) is a long term partnership that balances use of the Colorado River with the conservation of native species and their habitats. Implemented over a 50-year period, the program accommodates current water diversions and power production and will optimize opportunities for future water and power development by providing Endangered Species Act compliance through the implementation of a Habitat Conservation Plan. The program area extends over 400 miles of the lower Colorado River from Lake Mead to the southernmost border with Mexico. The Habitat Conservation Plan calls for the creation of over 8,100 acres of habitat for fish and wildlife species and the production of over 1.2 million native fish to augment existing populations. The plan will benefit at least 27 species, most of which are state or federally listed endangered, threatened, or sensitive species.

The Bureau of Reclamation is the implementing agency for the LCR MSCP Steering Committee and permittees which include state and Federal agencies, water and power users, municipalities, Native American tribes, conservation organizations, and other interested parties.

The LCR MSCP is unique for its scale, collaborative structure, and 50 year commitment, providing regulatory certainty for river operations while advancing science based, ecosystem wide conservation. This assistance listing supports activities that create, restore, and maintain habitat; conduct biological monitoring and research; and implement conservation actions identified in the program’s Habitat Conservation Plan. Award recipients typically include state wildlife agencies, universities, nonprofit organizations, and other entities working to conserve species affected by river operations.

overview.objective: The objective of this program is to develop and implement management strategies for the Las Vegas Wash to improve water quality, habitat integrity, and reduce the salinity and sediment transport while providing environmental enhancement and recreational opportunities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The objective of this program is to develop and implement management strategies for the Las Vegas Wash to improve water quality, habitat integrity, and reduce the salinity and sediment transport while providing environmental enhancement and recreational opportunities. The Las Vegas Wash Coordination Committee has decided that the SNWA will be the lead agency for receiving funding for this program due to the high costs and types of environmental improvement and enhancement, and ability to maintain restoration projects. The Las Vegas Wash Program plays an important role in environmental and water resource issues in Southern Nevada. Historically, the Las Vegas was an ephemeral stream carrying storm flows from the Las Vegas Valley to Lake Mead and the Colorado River. Urban development over the past 60 years has resulted in the formation of the wetlands that helped remove nutrients from these wastewater flows. As the rate of discharges increased, erosion also increased, gradually destroying the existing natural treatment systems and wildlife habitat and creating a large delta in the Las Vegas Bay of Lake Mead. Accelerating erosion, declining water quality, and loss habitat are some of the more pressing issues. Proposals submitted will be reviewed and awarded based on priority fulfillment of the 44 action items identified in the Plan and the availability of funding appropriations.

title: Cooperative Watershed Management
popularLongName: Cooperative Watershed Management Program or CWMP

overview.objective: Reclamation’s WaterSMART Cooperative Watershed Management program (CWMP) provides funding for the establishment or enlargement of grassroots, local watershed groups to encourage diverse stakeholders to develop collaborative solutions to address their water management needs. A watershed group is a self-sustaining, non-regulatory group that is composed of a diverse array of stakeholders, which may include, but is not limited to, private property owners, non-profit organizations, Federal, state, or local agencies, and tribes. Funding is provided on a competitive basis for the development of watershed groups, watershed restoration planning, and watershed management project planning and design. CWMP provides funding to local watershed groups to encourage diverse stakeholders to develop collaborative solutions to address their water management needs. Watershed groups bring together varied groups of stakeholders, some of which might otherwise be at odds, to provide a platform for collaborative, locally-led, and community-based water resource management. Stakeholders may initially unite around one issue that affects multiple stakeholder groups, for example food control or wildfire mitigation. However, these groups often evolve to have a more holistic approach: aiming to address multiple issues within the watershed and benefit a wide range of stakeholders.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Reclamation’s WaterSMART Cooperative Watershed Management program (CWMP) provides funding for the development of grassroots, local watershed groups to encourage diverse stakeholders to develop collaborative solutions to address their water management needs. A watershed group is a self-sustaining, non-regulatory group that is composed of a diverse array of stakeholders, which may include, but is not limited to, private property owners, non-profit organizations, Federal, State, or local agencies, and Tribes. Funding is provided on a competitive basis for the development of new and existing watershed groups, watershed restoration planning, and watershed management project design.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to an existing watershed group to digitize and consolidate existing water data, analyze and map potential watershed restoration projects by type and anticipated benefits, and engage with stakeholders to prioritize projects and update their watershed restoration plan. Reclamation also provided funding to a county to establish a new watershed group and conduct preplanning activities, including developing an organizational structure, stakeholder outreach and engagement, collecting data and consolidating data and consolidating existing information in the watershed, and identifying critical data gaps.

Reclamation provided funding to a watershed group that will work with stakeholders to design agricultural infrastructure upgrades and associated wetland restoration projects. Reclamation also provided funding to a nonprofit organization to establish a new watershed group and begin developing a watershed restoration plan. Activities include creating a steering committee, stakeholder outreach and engagement, and stakeholder workshops.

description: In their application, existing watershed groups must be able to demonstrate that they meet the definition of a watershed group under the Section 6002 of the Cooperative Watershed Management Act.

applicant.description: Existing watershed groups and entities sponsoring the establishment of a watershed group. The watershed group must be located in one of the following states or territories: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wyoming, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico. Existing watershed groups must meet the definition of a watershed group under Section 6002 of the Cooperative Watershed Management Act: the watershed group must be a grassroots, non-regulatory entity that addresses water availability and quality issues within the watershed and capable of promoting the sustainable use of water resources. The watershed group must make decisions on a consensus basis as identified in the by-laws of the watershed group and represent a diverse group of stakeholders, such as hydroelectric producers, livestock grazing, timber production, land development, recreation or tourism, irrigated agriculture, the environment, municipal water supplies, private property owners, Federal, state and local governments, and Tribes. Entities eligible to sponsor a new watershed group include States, Tribes, local or special districts (e.g., irrigation, water district, water conservation district), local governmental entities, interstate organizations, non-profit organizations, and institutes of higher education located in a state or territory identified above. The watershed group sponsor must also be able to significantly affect or be affected by the quality or quantity of water in the watershed and capable of promoting the sustainable use of water resources. A watershed group member or fiscal agent may apply on behalf of the watershed group if they are a state, Tribe, local or special district (e.g., irrigation, water district, water conservation district), local governmental entity, interstate organization, or a non-profit organization.

assistanceRestriction.description: The costs of administration and coordination under this program cannot exceed 20% of the total federal funding awarded. Stakeholder education/outreach and staff training are eligible activities if they are specifically linked to the proposed watershed group development, watershed restoration planning, or project design activities. Attending external conferences is limited to watershed group specific outreach and the cost . The cost of eligible conferences cannot exceed $5,000 per year. Monitoring, measurement, and fieldwork (e.g., water quality monitoring, vegetation surveys) to collect baseline information regarding the current conditions and needs of the watershed are eligible activities under this funding opportunity if they will inform a broader planning or design effort being completed as part of the same grant project and the costs do not exceed 50 percent of the total project cost. Each Notice of Funding Opportunity offered under the Cooperative Watershed Management Program includes specific information about ineligible activities.

overview.objective: The objective of the Applied Science Grants is to provide funding to non-Federal entities for the development of tools and information to support water management. Eligible projects include the development of modeling and forecasting tools, hydrologic data platforms, new data sets, and cloud seeding.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Applied Science Grants provides funding to non-Federal entities to improve access to and use of hydrologic data, develop and improve water management tools, and improve hydrologic modeling and forecasting capabilities. Water managers and reservoir operators rely on hydrologic data, modeling, and water supply forecasts to make decisions to meet future water demands. Water supply forecasts are estimates of current and future water supplies based on measured basin conditions (e.g., such as the quantity of upstream mountain snowpack). Results from these projects will be used by water managers to increase water supply reliability to meet water delivery requirements (e.g., compacts, decrees, etc.), provide flexibility in water operations to be more resilient during droughts, and enhance water supply forecasts to better predict floods and optimize limited water supplies. Example projects include improving operational models for irrigation water deliveries or reservoir operations, improving the use of snow monitoring technologies to enhance the skill of water supply forecasts, and improving data acquisition, data analysis, and data delivery, including the development of hydrologic databases.

title: New Mexico Rio Grande Basin Pueblos Irrigation Infrastructure

overview.objective: Rehabilitate and repair irrigation infrastructure of the Rio Grande Pueblos to conserve water and help address potential conflicts over water in the Rio Grande Basin.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
Under the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009, Congress authorized $4 million to conduct a study of the irrigation infrastructure within the 18 Rio Grande pueblos, and $6 million in each of ten subsequent years to address identified infrastructure improvements. The Act required a study report to be submitted to Congress including a list of projects recommended for implementation.

Initially, detailed physical surveys of the existing irrigation infrastructure at each pueblo were completed. Most of the surveys have now been completed but remaining areas will be surveyed as specific project need arises.

The study report identified nearly $280 million in irrigation improvements, at a 2017 pricing level, needed on pueblo lands. These improvements are important to the Tribal economies, to preserving their cultural traditions for future generations, and to maximize water conservation in the Rio Grande Basin.

The report was finalized in June 2022 and submitted to Congress by the Department of the Interior's Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs. Since that time, the program has received consistent funding and projects continue to be implemented on tribal lands throughout the Rio Grande Basin. While the authorizing legislation expired in 2019, it continues to be extended annually within Reclamation's budget pending long-term reauthorization.

The ecosystem there is dependent on a balance of saltwater from the San Francisco Bay and freshwater from the Sacramento River and the San Joaquin River. title: Implementation of the Taos Pueblo Indian water rights settlement

overview.objective:
The Claims Resolution Act of 2010 was signed into law on December 8, 2010, authorizing the settlement of two long-running New Mexico Indian water rights cases.  Title V, the Taos Pueblo Indian Water Rights Settlement Act, authorizes implementation of the Abeyta (Taos Pueblo) settlement.  The Settlement Act authorizes and directs the Bureau of Reclamation to provide financial assistance in the form of grants on a non-reimbursable basis to plan, permit, design, engineer, and construct Mutual-Benefit Projects that will minimize adverse effects on the Pueblo’s water resources by moving future non-Indian ground water pumping away from the Pueblo’s Buffalo Pasture, a culturally sensitive wetland.  The Federal Team is working with the Mutual-Benefit Project parties as they get ready for the on-the-ground phase of settlement implementation. Reclamation’s Albuquerque Area Office is in the process of completing environmental compliance and awarding grants to the entities that are moving forward with their projects.

The overall cost of the settlement is $144 million, of which $124 million would be paid by the Federal government and $20 million by the State of New Mexico. The total federal contribution of $124 million includes $88.0 million directed to the Bureau of Indian Affairs for the Taos Pueblo Water Development Fund, and a $36 million settlement fund ($16 million mandatory and $20 million discretionary funds) directed to Reclamation for the Mutual-Benefit Projects.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Abeyta Settlement Agreement is a landmark water rights settlement in the Taos Valley, New Mexico, resolving long-standing disputes over water rights in the Rio Hondo and Rio Pueblo de Taos systems. overview.assistanceListingDescription: The program is designed to improve water reliability, strengthen water supplies, and foster resilience to drought conditions within the Colorado River Basin. Funding comes from two major federal laws—the Inflation Reduction Act and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act—which support modernizing water infrastructure, expanding and enhancing water supplies, and restoring ecosystems or habitats. Targeted support backs projects that address challenges from strained water sources by strengthening conservation practices and enhancing sustainability. Investments in planning, design, and construction enable communities to use water more efficiently and ensure reliable supplies over time, helping to reduce pressure on existing systems, improve drought preparedness, and promote responsible stewardship of water resources. Assistance Listing 15.567 is available to state, Tribal, regional, and local public entities that manage water resources. This program stands out by combining two historic federal investments, accelerating projects that bring both immediate and long-term benefits to areas facing drought.

overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Water Education Foundation has developed several programs and publications that educate various audiences on the importance of water resources in California, including the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta.

list.description: In Fiscal Year 2025, Reclamation funded the Water Education Foundation to deliver educational programs that increased public understanding of California's water resources, the Bay-Delta watershed, and Reclamation's mission. Activities included developing and distributing educational publications, hosting workshops and conferences for water professionals and stakeholders, conducting teacher training and student education programs, supporting public tours and field-based learning opportunities, and producing digital content highlighting current water management challenges and collaborative solutions. These efforts helped improve awareness of complex water management issues and fostered informed engagement among educators, students, decision-makers, and the public.

In Fiscal Year 2026, Reclamation is continuing to fund the Water Education Foundation to expand educational and outreach opportunities focused on California water management and the Bay-Delta watershed. Planned activities will include educational publications, professional workshops and conferences, teacher and student education programs, public tours, and multimedia resources designed to increase understanding of water infrastructure, ecosystem restoration, water reliability, and collaborative resource management. These efforts are expected to provide timely, science-based information to educators, stakeholders, and the public while supporting informed decision-making and greater awareness of Reclamation's role in managing California's water resources.

list.description: The Water Education Foundation completed several 2024–2025 initiatives, including launching the Klamath River Basin Tour, which explored dam removal sites and watershed areas in California and Oregon while addressing water supply, quality, agriculture, tribal history, and habitat restoration through diverse speakers. The Foundation updated its Klamath Basin Map to reflect current rivers, lakes, reservoirs, farmland, urban areas, reservations, and dam removal sites, along with explanations of major water and habitat issues. Its main website was refreshed and adapted for mobile access, offering videos, story maps, news feeds, and an expanded multilingual format, with staff trained for ongoing maintenance. The Aquapedia online water encyclopedia was overhauled to provide streamlined, up-to-date, and vetted information on key California and western water issues, including Delta topics and Reclamation facilities. Additionally, the Layperson’s Guide to California Water was revised with current data on water history, drought and flood management, delivery systems, Delta challenges, water rights, and conservation options, and a Spanish edition was published to improve accessibility for broader audiences.

In FY26, accomplishments include progress on the Layperson’s Guide to Flood Management, delivery of Project WET workshops, and implementation of multiple water tours, including the Bay-Delta tour. Additional work will advance the Impact Video and Water Network Initiative, expand public outreach and improving understanding of water management in the Delta and statewide.

overview.objective: The objective of the Agricultural Water Conservation Efficiency Program is to invite eligible applicants to leverage their money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation on projects that save water, improve water management, increase water supply reliability, improve energy efficiency, and benefit endangered species. Projects that achieve this by directly enabling on-farm water conservation or water use efficiency projects that can be undertaken by farmers and ranchers remain a high priority for this program. Reclamation and the USDA's Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) are encouraging water suppliers to work with farmers to identify the roles at play to facilitate and/or assist with on-farm improvements that contribute to water supply reliability in the State of California.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
Invite Indian tribes, irrigation districts, water districts, and other organizations with water or power delivery authority to leverage their money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation on projects that seek to:
•	Conserve and use agricultural water more efficiently, 
•	Mitigate conflict risk in areas at a high risk of future water conflict,
•	Enable farmers to make on-farm improvements that may be eligible for USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) funding, and
•	Contribute benefits to water supply reliability in the Western United States.

Project sponsors leverage their money and resources by cost-sharing with Reclamation to construct on-farm projects that save water, improve water management, increase water supply reliability, improve energy efficiency, and benefit endangered species.  

Funded projects result in quantifiable and sustained agricultural water savings and support broader water reliability benefits.  The AWUE program supports Reclamation’s priorities, including:
•	Increasing agricultural water supplies, 
•	Leveraging science and technology to improve water supply reliability for farmers, and
•	Addressing drought impacts on agricultural activities.

overview.objective: Section 4007 of Public Law 114-322, also known as The Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) Act allows the Secretary of the Interior to negotiate and enter into an agreement on behalf of the United States for the design, study and construction or expansion of federally owned or State-led water storage project. The Secretary may participate in a federally owned storage project “in an amount equal to not more than 50 percent of the total cost of the federally owned storage project,” (4007(b)(2)) and may participate in a State-led storage project “in an amount equal to not more than 25 percent of the total cost of the State-led storage project” (4007(c)(1)). In return for this cost-share, “at least a proportional share of the project benefits are the Federal benefits, including water supplies dedicated to specific purposes such as environmental enhancement and wildlife refuges” (4007(c)(2)(C)). To be eligible for funding, the Secretary of the Interior must have determined the project to be feasible before January 1, 2021.

Reclamation will proceed with expenditure of construction funding once a project has been found feasible, a cost sharing agreement has been signed with a non-Federal partner for a construction project, all appropriate regulatory and contractual requirements have been met, and the project has been named in appropriations legislation.

overview.objective: The objective of the Aquatic Ecosystem Restoration Program is to work cooperatively with states, Tribes, and other entities as they study, design and construct aquatic ecosystem restoration projects that are collaboratively developed, have widespread regional benefits, and result in the improvement of the health of fisheries, wildlife, and aquatic habitat through restoration and improved fish passage. As used here, “aquatic ecosystem” refers to freshwater and brackish water habitats such as lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, wetlands, swamps, and estuaries and the adjacent floodplains, riparian corridors, deltas, and shallow aquifers that interact with surface water.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Aquatic Ecosystems Restoration Program provides cost-shared financial assistance for the study, design and construction of aquatic ecosystem restoration projects that are collaboratively developed, have widespread regional benefits, and result in the improvement of the health of fisheries, wildlife, and aquatic habitat through restoration and improved fish passage. Reclamation has established a merit-based process to allocate funding that includes the competitive WaterSMART Aquatic Ecosystem Restoration Projects funding opportunity and a non-competitive (discretionary) process to allocate funding for emergent needs related to Commissioner’s Office priorities.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to a city to complete the study and design of an aquatic ecosystem restoration project that includes the replacement of an undersized bridge, removal of abandoned irrigation infrastructure, restoration of the floodplain, improve fish passage and habitat for steelhead trout and Coho salmon, and the development of plans for a park to increase recreational opportunity. reduction and floodplain restoration project near the confluence of two rivers. Reclamation provided funding to an irrigation district to remove their existing rotary drum fish screens and install flat plate screens and a traveling screen cleaning system to improve fish passage and reduce entrainment of ESA-listed fish species. This project is one element of a larger regional effort by irrigation districts in the state to modernize and improve aging infrastructure to conserve water and improve conditions for aquatic species.

Reclamation provided funding to a Tribe to construct instream habitat for the benefit of ESA-listed Coho Salmon and reconnect a 1-mile segment of the river to its historic floodplain. The Tribe will construct numerous habitat features, including 5-acre of new floodplain habitat and, one acre of constructed riffle and incorporate beneficial channel fill and low flow channel modification.

overview.objective: The Desalination Construction Program provides up to 25 percent cost-shared financial assistance for entities to plan, design, and/or construct ocean or brackish water desalination facilities. Desalination projects help communities to diversify their water supply portfolio by providing new sources of local water supply.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The WaterSMART: Desalination Construction Projects funding opportunity invites eligible applicants to submit proposals for the planning, design, and/or construction of facilities to desalinate seawater or brackish surface water or groundwater. By providing communities with new sources of local water supply, desalination projects diversify the water supply portfolio, increase water management flexibility during times of shortage, and make the water supply more reliable.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to a water district to construct an ocean water desalination facility located at Doheny State Beach in California. The project will create a drought resistant and reliable source of potable drinking water for the region, reduce dependence on imported water, and provide for an emergency water supply in event of a natural disaster or disruption of service to imported water. Project components include a subsurface slant well intake system, seawater conveyance, a seawater desalination plant, brine disposal through an existing wastewater ocean outfall, solids handling facilities, and potable water distribution infrastructure. Once completed, the project will have a capacity of 5,321 acre-feet per year of potable water.

title: WaterSMART Planning and Project Design Grants

overview.objective: To provide cost-shared funding for collaborative planning and design projects that support water management improvements. This includes funding to (1) conduct planning activities and develop a strategy to improve water supplies, including drought resiliency planning and water marketing; and (2) to develop site-specific designs for construction projects that improve water supplies and/or water management.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The objective of the Planning and Project Design Grants program is to leverage money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation for initial, or early-stage planning activities to identify and prioritize potential projects that will improve water supplies, water management, drought resiliency, and other water resources enhancement projects, and to develop a strategy document for the implementation of those projects. The program also provides cost share funding for the final design of on-the-ground water supply, water management, drought resiliency, and multi-purpose watershed management construction projects that are eligible for construction funding under 15.507 WaterSMART Water and Energy Efficiency Grants, 15.514 Drought Resiliency Projects, and 15.579 Enhancing Water Resources Projects.

list.description: Reclamation provided funding to an irrigation district to design the conversion of a 30,000-foot section of the district’s lateral from an open ditch to a closed, pressurized pipe system. The project, once constructed, will conserve an estimated 2,233 acre-feet of water annually. Reclamation provided funding to a city to develop a water strategy that will address the depletion of groundwater resources, the primary source of culinary water in the area. Through this planning effort, the city will evaluate the potential for water reuse, groundwater recharge, and water conservation to sustainably manage groundwater resources.

Reclamation provided funding to a water agency to design a permanent turnout to convey water to a recharge basin. The project once constructed the new turnout will increase groundwater storage capacity and water supply reliability. Reclamation also provided funding to a water district to develop a water strategy for the implementation of  projects that will improve water quality, identify water supply alternatives and increase water conservation.

assistanceUsage.description: Planning activities eligible for funding for the development of a water strategy include outreach and partnership building; technical analyses, scoping, and other planning activities described in the Notice of Funding Opportunity. Project design activities eligible for funding include developing project requirements and evaluating design alternatives; evaluating site alternatives and selecting the project site; preparing final design drawings and specifications for construction; evaluating economic conditions, preparing project cost estimates and developing a project implementation plan; conducting biological and cultural resource surveys; researching legal and institutional requirements such as land ownership and easements; and other design-related activities described in the Notice of Funding Opportunity.

assistanceRestriction.description: Activities that are not eligible for funding include the design of projects considered normal operations, maintenance, and replacement; pilot projects and studies to evaluate technical capability, economic feasibility, or viability for full-scale implementation or to test an unproven material or technology; and planning and design activities related to on-farm improvements. Each Notice of Funding Opportunity offered under this listing provides specific information about ineligible project types and activities.  Monitoring, measurement, and other fieldwork costs are generally limited to 30% of the total project costs or the amount specified in the funding opportunity. The costs to develop decision support tools are limited to 30% of the total project costs or the amount specified in the funding opportunity.  Legal costs are also limited to the activities specified in the funding opportunity and cannot exceed the amount specified in the opportunity.

overview.objective: To identify and provide information needed to sustain subsistence fisheries and wildlife management on Federal public lands, for rural Alaskans, through a multidisciplinary, collaborative program. Two programs are administered under the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) to fulfill this objective. The Fisheries Resource Monitoring Program (Monitoring Program) funds approximately 40 studies annually to provide information on stock status and trends, harvests, and traditional ecological knowledge to manage and regulate Federal subsistence fisheries. The Partners for Fisheries Monitoring Program (Partners Program) strengthens Alaska Native and rural involvement in subsistence fisheries management and research. The program provides funds directly to Alaska Native and rural organizations to hire fishery biologists, social scientists, and educators with the intent of increasing the organizations ability to participate in Federal Subsistence Management.

awardProcedure.description:
For the Monitoring Program, an interagency technical review committee evaluates proposals based on the criteria outlined in the request for federal assistance. The committee develops a draft monitoring plan from the highest priority projects, based on their technical review and available funding. The draft monitoring plan is reviewed by 10 regional advisory councils and the public. An interagency staff committee reviews all comments and provides recommendations. The Federal Subsistence Board reviews all comments and provides a recommendation. Final selection of projects is conducted by the Office of Subsistence Management (OSM) Assistant Regional Director based on recommendations and available funding. Funding of the Monitoring Plan is administered by OSM. 
For the Partners Program, an interagency review committee with external commentators is formed to evaluate proposals. The interagency committee members make recommendations for funding. The evaluations are based on the criteria outlined in the request for federal assistance. The proposals are ranked and the highest-ranking proposals are funded by OSM, based on available funding. Final selection of projects is conducted by the OSM Assistant Regional Director based on recommendations and available funding. Funding of the Partners Program is administered by OSM. 
Applicants will be notified of review results by either issuing a fully executed Award either electronically or through the mail, or by sending written notification to the applicant that the application will not be funded.

overview.objective:
Provide financial assistance for projects for the effective, long-term conservation of African rhino populations and their habitats. The objectives are to increase population growth, management and governance improvements at key rhino sites, and to develop greater national leadership and capacity, stakeholder collaboration,  

and effective CITES implementation in key rhino range states. This program supports projects that prioritize direct site-based conservation actions for Key 1 and Key 2 populations and other populations that are important to the survival of critically endangered black rhinoceros. Project work occurs within rhinoceros range and show clear relevance to rhinoceros field conservation actions, identify immediate threats to rhinoceros survival and support direct conservation activities to eliminate or reduce those threats, address biological management of rhinoceros populations, demonstrate how they address regional and national rhinoceros management plans, develop capacity, and implement CITES.

overview.objective: The QZAP program funds projects towards the fulfillment of the top priorities in the Quagga/Zebra Mussel Action Plan for Western U.S. Waters (QZAP 2.0) and will be limited to states within the boundaries of the Western Regional Panel within the United States.  Projects may address limiting the spread of invasive mussels through: 1) Protecting western ecosystems through support and/or establishment of prevention programs for invasive mussels at identified high risk control points, 2) Limiting the spread of invasive mussels through containment by increasing compliance with federal, state, local and tribal laws; 3) Increasing the effectiveness of outreach and education efforts to help advance prevention efforts; 4) Building capacity to detect and respond to new invasive mussel infestations; and 5) Conducting Research that benefits the priorities listed above, including (but not limited to) social science research to evaluate the effectiveness of invasive species prevention messaging.

title: Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act

overview.objective: To provide grants to museums to assist in the consultation on and documentation of Native American human remains and cultural items; to provide grants to Indian tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations, as defined in the Act, to assist in identifying human remains and cultural items; and to provide grants to museums, Indian tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations to assist in the repatriation of human remains and cultural items.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) Grants provides funding to help museums, federally recognized Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations consult on, document, and return Native American human remains and cultural items with cultural significance. This program supports the repatriation process, covering activities like consultation, travel, transportation, contamination removal, reburial, storage, and related staff time.

list.description:
1) Repatriation and Return Activities - These projects focus on safely and respectfully returning ancestors or cultural items.

2) Consultation & Collaboration Projects - These projects help communities and institutions work together to plan returns and resolve cultural questions.

3) Documentation & Research Projects - These projects gather information needed to determine origin, cultural connection, or proper treatment.

4) Preparation and Care of Collections - These projects ensure items are properly handled before, during, or after consultation.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects to museums, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations to assist in consultation, documentation and repatriation under NAGPRA.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: 1) Repatriation of Ancestral Remains: a museum successfully repatriated the remains of numerous ancestors and associated funerary objects to a Native American tribe. This effort involved careful coordination, respectful handling, and a meaningful reburial ceremony, providing closure and honoring the cultural heritage of the tribe. 2) Cultural Consultation and Documentation: An academic institution collaborated with various tribes to document and catalog cultural items from a significant archaeological site. This project involved detailed consultations, updating inventories, and ensuring that cultural items were accurately identified and documented, facilitating future repatriation efforts. 3) Collaborative Projects: A tribal council worked with multiple museums to repatriate culturally significant items. These collaborative efforts ensured that items were returned to their rightful communities, where they could be reintegrated into cultural practices and ceremonies.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects to museums, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations to assist in consultation, documentation and repatriation under NAGPRA.

For repatriation grants, publication under 43 CFR Part 10 of a Notice of Inventory Completion or Notice of Intent to Repatriate in the Federal Register is required.

Such term does not include the Smithsonian Institution or any other Federal agency. [25 USC 3001 (8)].

Indian Tribe: Any tribe, band, nation, or other organized group or community of Indians, including any Alaska Native village (as defined in, or established pursuant to, the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act), which is recognized as eligible for the special programs and services provided by the United States to Indians because of their status as Indians. [25 USC 3001 (7)]. The Department of the Interior has interpreted this definition as applying to over 560 Indian tribes and Alaska Native villages that are recognized by the United States Government. This list does not include Alaska regional or village corporations, although Alaska Native villages may subcontract work under grants to such corporations. 

Native Hawaiian Organization: Any organization which serves and represents the interests of Native Hawaiians, has as a primary and stated purpose the provision of services to Native Hawaiians, and has expertise in Native Hawaiian affairs, and shall include the Office of Hawaiian Affairs and Hui Malama I Na Kupuna O Hawai'i Nei. assistanceUsage.description:
Grant funds must be used for CONSULTATION, DOCUMENTATION, or REPATRIATION under NAGPRA.  

Consultation and documentation projects should lead to determining control, treatment, and disposition of NAGPRA cultural items. Consultation projects support efforts related to compiling or revising a NAGPRA inventory and making or responding to requests for items in a NAGPRA summary. Documentation projects support determining the geographical origin, cultural affiliation, and other basic facts surrounding the acquisition of Native American cultural items. 

Repatriation means the transfer of control of Native American human remains and/or cultural items to lineal descendants, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations.  Repatriation includes disposition of culturally unidentifiable Native American human remains (CUI) according to 43 C.F.R. 10.11. Repatriation projects defray costs associated with the packaging, transportation, contamination removal, reburial, and/or storage of NAGPRA-related human remains and/or cultural items.

title: National Center for Preservation Technology and Training

overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports projects that develop innovative tools, materials, and methods for preserving historic buildings, landscapes, and cultural resources across the United States. The National Park Service’s National Center for Preservation Technology and Training (NCPTT) partners with public institutions, governments, and educational organizations to advance the field of preservation and make new technologies more accessible to practitioners and the public. What makes this program unique is its focus on innovation. Funded projects are expected to push the preservation field forward—developing new methods, adapting emerging technologies, or finding creative ways to share preservation knowledge widely.

list.description:
1) Research and Innovation - Projects include researchers studying how large technology facilities can be designed so they do not disrupt important community views and sounds, such as historic farms, old buildings, monuments, and outdoor art;  a team testing a new way to visualize and honor gravesites by creating digital models, helping families and communities remember and learn about them; and experts developing new imaging methods to help preserve historic photographic prints and plates by testing polarized and multispectral imaging techniques.

2) Technology Development - Projects include developers creating a mobile app that uses interactive storytelling and language technology to guide building owners and renters through the steps to check and repair historic buildings after a flood; and researchers creating an artificial‑intelligence‑based system that monitors how historic buildings are used so caretakers can better plan for their future.

3)  Digital Documentation and Visualization - Projects include a research team using drones to safely map the inside of old buildings that are too dangerous to enter, creating digital models that help experts understand structural conditions and plan preservation work.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that support innovative research and training projects that advance the practice of historic preservation. The goal is to fund cultural resource projects that will create better tools, better materials, and better approaches for protecting historic buildings and landscapes, and other significant cultural resources.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award
Discretionary and Non-Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Advancing Research That Protects Community Heritage - Researchers created new ways to design and operate high‑tech facilities so they do not harm the treasured views and soundscapes that matter to local communities. Their work helps protect scenic landscapes, historic farms, older buildings, monuments, outdoor sculptures, cemeteries, and historic battlefields.

2) Building Tools That Make Preservation Easier for the Public - A university team developed a user-friendly mobile app that guides building owners, renters, and managers through the steps to inspect and recover historic buildings after floods. The app uses interactive storytelling and language technology to make complex instructions simple and accessible.

3) Innovative Digital Documentation of Historic Places - Researchers used drones to safely map the interiors of historic structures that are too dangerous or unstable to enter. They produced detailed blueprints and digital models that help experts understand structural conditions and plan preservation work. Funding also supported early work on digital visualization techniques that allow families and communities to better understand and honor historic gravesites.

3) Improving Care for Historic Materials - Scientists tested new imaging methods to help preserve historic photographic prints and plates. By experimenting with polarized and multispectral imaging, they produced practical information that can help museums and archives protect important photographs for future generations.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that support innovative research and training projects that advance the practice of historic preservation. The goal is to fund cultural resource projects that will create better tools, better materials, and better approaches for protecting historic buildings and landscapes, and other significant cultural resources.

overview.objective: The National Maritime Heritage Grants Program provides matching grants for education and preservation projects designed to preserve historic maritime resources and to increase public awareness and appreciation for the maritime heritage of the United States. The grants will help State, Tribal, and local governments and private nonprofit organizations preserve and interpret their maritime heritage.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The National Maritime Heritage Grants provide 1-to-1 matching funds for a wide range of preservation and education projects in three broad categories: Historic Maritime Properties, Maritime Heritage Collections, and Traditional Maritime Skills. Grant projects are intended to help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.

list.description:
1) Education & Public Awareness: Funding may support projects that help people learn about the nation’s maritime past. This can include creating exhibits, programs, or community activities that explain how ships, waterways, and maritime travel shaped history. Grants may also help organizations develop workshops, teaching materials, or digital content that make maritime stories accessible to the public.

2) Preservation & Conservation: Funds may be used to protect and care for historic maritime resources. This could involve repairing or stabilizing vessels, artifacts, and archaeological collections, or performing engineering studies and scientific tests to understand their condition. Projects may focus on preserving materials so they can be safely exhibited, researched, or passed on to future generations.

3) Research & Documentation: Grants may support efforts to document and study maritime sites and collections. This includes researching underwater archaeological areas, examining historical records, and creating detailed documentation of artifacts or structures. These projects help deepen understanding and ensure accurate interpretation of maritime heritage.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Preserving Important Maritime History - Funding through this program has helped protect and conserve historic ships, maritime structures, and archaeological collections. Support has been used to carry out engineering studies, stabilize fragile materials, and complete conservation work so historic maritime resources can be safely preserved and shared with future generations. These efforts keep irreplaceable pieces of maritime history intact and accessible.

2) Expanding Public Access to Maritime Heritage - Awards have enabled public agencies and organizations to create exhibits, rehabilitate collections, and open more maritime materials for viewing, research, and education. By improving displays, enhancing storage and interpretation, and increasing access to coastal or underwater archaeological resources, the program helps the public better understand and appreciate the nation’s maritime past.

3) Supporting Community Learning and Education - The program has funded educational initiatives that bring maritime stories to communities across the country. These projects include developing teaching materials, creating public programs, and supporting cultural organizations in sharing the role of waterways, seafaring, and coastal industries in shaping national history.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.
