list.description:
1) Preserving Historic Places - Historic buildings and structures are being reinforced and restored to ensure they remain safe and accessible for future generations, and conservation work is helping maintain the integrity of culturally significant sites, from historic ranches to traditional gathering areas.

2) Investing in Future Leaders - students and early-career professionals are gaining real-world experience in archaeology, museum work, and archives management.

3) Uncovering Untold Histories - Studies are being conducted to document the experiences of indigenous peoples, and oral histories and local knowledge are being integrated into public interpretation and educational materials.

4) Strengthening Tribal Partnerships - Tribal governments are working alongside federal agencies to manage and protect culturally important resources.

5) Expanding Public Access - Archival materials and museum collections are being digitized and made available online, reaching audiences around the world.

1) Preserving and Sharing History - Funding has digitized historic photographs and rare documents, making them accessible online for students, teachers, researchers, and lifelong learners. Fragile albums, scrapbooks, and museum objects have been stabilized and rehoused in archival storage, ensuring their preservation for future generations.  

2) Protecting Archaeological and Historic Sites - Projects have surveyed and documented archaeological sites, including areas impacted by wildfires or floods, producing maps, inventories, photographs, and condition assessments that inform protection and future planning. Collections have been organized into archival-quality storage with clear tracking, ensuring long-term preservation and accountability. Baseline studies and compliance reports have been completed or updated, supporting resource management and historic preservation.

3) Engaging Communities and Tribal Nations - Collaborative projects have co-created research and interpretation with Indigenous educators and Tribal partners, centering traditional knowledge and ensuring respectful storytelling in public programs. Ceremonies and repatriation work have strengthened stewardship and collaboration, while artist residencies and demonstrations have connected visitors directly with makers and knowledge holders. Community workshops and outreach have improved trust and co-stewardship.

4) Building Workforce Skills - Apprentices, interns, and research associates have gained hands-on experience in archives, museums, archaeology, and historic trades. Training in carpentry, masonry, metalwork, roofing, arboriculture, and collections care has supported maintenance and stabilization of culturally significant structures and landscapes, strengthening career pathways and increasing capacity for preservation work.

title: National Fire Plan-Wildland Urban Interface Community Fire Assistance

overview.objective: To assist communities at risk from catastrophic wildland fires by providing assistance in the following areas: community programs that develop local capability including; assessment and planning, mitigation activities, and community and homeowner education and action; plan and implement hazardous fuels reduction activities, monitoring or maintenance associated with such hazardous fuels reduction activities, on federal land, or on adjacent nonfederal land for activities that mitigate the threat of catastrophic fire to communities and natural resources in high risk areas; enhance local and small business employment opportunities for rural communities; enhance the knowledge and fire protection capability of rural fire districts by providing assistance in education, and mitigation methods on a cost share basis; and implementing the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports communities that are at risk from devastating wildland fires by helping them strengthen their local fire resilience and preparedness. The program provides funding for community-led efforts such as wildfire risk assessments, local mitigation planning, and education that helps residents understand how to protect their homes and neighborhoods. It also supports projects that reduce hazardous vegetation and fuels, either in nearby federal areas or on surrounding non-federal lands, to lessen the threat of severe fires in high‑risk regions. In addition, the program boosts opportunities for rural workers and small businesses and improves the capabilities of local fire districts through training and modern approaches to wildfire prevention. Through these combined efforts, the program advances the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy while empowering communities, Tribal governments, states, local agencies, schools, and nonprofit organizations to build safer, more fire‑adapted places.

list.description: Funded projects focus on protecting communities and natural resources from catastrophic wildfires, including clearing hazardous vegetation along roads and trails to reduce fuel for wildfires; creating defensible space around historic structures and park facilities; conducting brush removal, pile burning, and firebreak maintenance.

Funding supports work that reduces wildfire danger and protects important historic places by cleaning up overgrown vegetation and maintaining healthier landscapes. Crews create safe buffer zones around buildings, clear brush and fallen limbs, and chip or remove dense vegetation along fences and fire breaks. These activities help safeguard cultural treasures, improve wildlife habitat, and lower the chance that intense wildfires will damage natural areas or structures.

title: National Park Service Conservation, Protection, Outreach, and Education

overview.objective:
This program supports projects complementary to National Park Service program efforts in natural and cultural resource conservation, protection, and environmental sustainability. 

This program funds projects that support the mission of the National Park Service but are not covered under other specific programs.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
This program supports projects that help care for and protect the natural and cultural resources found on public lands while expanding opportunities for people to learn about and enjoy these places. Funding may be used for activities such as restoring habitats, preserving historic features, improving visitor access, and offering educational programs that connect communities with nature, history, and science. The program also helps strengthen environmental sustainability by supporting projects that reduce impacts to sensitive resources and promote responsible outdoor recreation.
This assistance listing serves a broad group of partners, including nonprofit organizations, government entities, industry groups, researchers, and members of the public who benefit from healthier landscapes, improved access, and expanded learning opportunities.

list.description:
1)	Educational and Professional Development: Projects support teacher professional development and the creation of educational materials for distance learning, helping educators integrate public lands into their curriculum.
2)	Public Engagement and Interpretation: Funds are used to develop programs that enhance visitor enjoyment, promote interpretation of natural and cultural resources, and increase public understanding of conservation issues.
3)	Visitor Services and Transportation: Awards finance shuttle operations in high-visitation areas to reduce environmental impacts and improve access, such as those servicing forest or coastal sites.
4)	Restoration and Stewardship: Funding is directed to nonprofit partnerships for hands-on restoration work, habitat improvement, and trail maintenance to improve ecological health and visitor safety.
5)	Cultural Enrichment and Recreation: Funding may cover live music or interpretive performances to enrich visitor experiences and foster community engagement in recreational spaces.

1) Education, engagement, and access - Outdoor recreation experiences for students and military families. Facilitated trips introduce people to activities like fishing, camping, hiking, paddling, and biking, while reducing barriers such as transportation and gear. Public events provide youth‑friendly activities and demonstrations that spark interest in aviation and science.

2) Transportation and visitor services - Funding supports a visitor shuttle so sites don’t have to close when parking fills; the service expands access and improves the experience for everyone. Transit programs ease congestion, improve accessibility, and allow visitors to bring bikes or boats—reducing traffic, improving air quality, and enhancing safety.

3) Stewardship, conservation, and safety - Trail care and public‑space cleanup. Staff coordinate with site managers to remove debris and graffiti, manage vegetation, repair trail surfaces, and support safe enjoyment of historic places. Projects sample for invasive mussels, educate boaters, and conduct inspections to keep waterways healthy during high‑use seasons. Teams help with invasive species control, habitat assessments, long‑term monitoring, and restoration—building skills while advancing stewardship goals. Partnerships operate river gages and temperature sensors that provide long‑term data used for water supply management, water‑quality tracking, and flood planning.

4) National celebrations and public events - Funding supports widely viewed programs featuring orchestral performances for Memorial Day and Independence Day, for the benefit of millions. A multi‑day public event brings historic ships for parades and activities that highlight national history and strengthen international partnerships.

list.description: Assistance Listing 15.954 supports a wide range of community-driven projects that connect people to public lands. It funds teacher training and educational materials that bring parks into classrooms, helping students learn about nature and history from anywhere. Funds also support programs that enhance the visitor experience—like guided tours and exhibits that explain the importance of conservation. In busy parks, the program helps fund shuttle services to ease traffic and protect sensitive areas. It also backs restoration work led by nonprofits, improving trails, habitats, and overall safety. Cultural events like live music and performances funded through this program enrich visits and build stronger community ties to public lands.

In 2026, this program supported a wide range of projects that strengthened conservation, expanded public access, deepened community partnerships, and improved understanding of natural and cultural resources across the country. Funding helped protect waterways by preventing the spread of invasive aquatic species and supporting monitoring efforts that keep rivers and lakes healthy for wildlife and recreation. Important restoration work continued in forested and mountainous areas, where specialists collected data, planted native vegetation, assessed post‑fire conditions, and improved habitat resilience in the face of drought and wildfires.

Many achievements centered on improving visitor access and enhancing outdoor experiences. Transportation projects expanded shuttle services and public transit options, reducing congestion, improving air quality, and helping hundreds of thousands of visitors reach popular destinations safely. Parks strengthened emergency services, maintained fee‑collection operations, and improved trails and landscapes to ensure safe, enjoyable recreation for all. Educational programs introduced thousands of students and military families to outdoor activities like hiking, camping, and science-based exploration, helping people overcome barriers and feel welcome in public lands. Teachers received training to incorporate park science into classroom lessons, and youth participated in internships focused on resource management, and ecosystem stewardship.
Cultural and historic preservation also saw significant progress. Projects safeguarded historic structures, supported community-centered museum initiatives, delivered large public America 250 celebrations of national heritage, and expanded engagement.

title: Cooperative Management of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve.

overview.objective: The objectives of this program focus on the cooperative management, administration, and protection of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve. They include overseeing land and facilities, administering conservation programs, and ensuring compliance with preservation measures. The work also involves coordinating with local governments, entering into partnerships and contracts, and securing funding to support the reserve’s long-term stewardship and public engagement.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve is a unique place where history, rural landscapes, natural beauty, and community come together. Through this financial assistance program, the National Park Service works in partnership with the State of Washington and local governments to support the cooperative management of the Reserve, as directed by Public Law 95‑625. The program exists to help ensure that the Reserve’s historic farms, scenic views, cultural resources, recreational opportunities, and natural environments are protected and maintained for the benefit of the public. Unlike many national park units, Ebey’s Landing is managed through a shared governance model. The National Park Service can transfer certain management responsibilities to state or local partners, provide technical assistance, and offer supplemental funding to support day‑to‑day operations, long‑term preservation, and visitor services. These cooperative agreements strengthen local stewardship, allow communities to directly shape how the Reserve is cared for, and ensure that its rural heritage remains a living part of Island County.

title: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund
popularLongName: HPF Disaster Relief Program; Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund Grants (ESHPF)

overview.objective: The objectives of this supplemental funding is to provide for necessary expenses related to the consequences of disasters, including costs to States, Tribes, and territories. Funds may be used for historic and cultural resource preservation work in the program areas defined by the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) and that meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. Capacity, technical assistance, and emergency repairs to historic and archeological resources impacted by disasters, consistent with legislative intent, may be funded. Funding should substantially mitigate disaster caused damage and mitigate future risk.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This Assistance Listing provides disaster recovery grants to support the preservation and repair of historic and cultural resources listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or equivalent Tribal register. Funding may be used for preservation work eligible under the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) that also meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. Eligible projects include physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administrative and capacity support within areas receiving major disaster declarations. Funding should substantially mitigate disaster-caused damage and future risk.

list.description: No new awards were funded in FY 2025.

1) Emergency stabilization and repairs - Stabilizing historic buildings: Shoring up walls, roofs, and foundations; addressing water intrusion; and performing immediate repairs so structures don’t deteriorate further after storms, floods, or fires. Repairing community landmarks: Fixing damage to historic hospitals, theaters, hotels, and other public‑serving buildings so they can safely host visitors, programs, and services again.

2) Planning and assessments - Damage assessments and preservation planning: Hiring engineers and preservation specialists to inspect historic promenades, buildings, and cultural sites after declared disasters; documenting conditions and prioritizing repairs so places can reopen safely. Pre‑preservation work: Creating scopes of work, schedules, and cost estimates; coordinating with local stakeholders to plan repairs and conservation activities that meet preservation standards.

3) District‑wide recovery - Commercial district rehabilitation: Stabilizing and repairing groups of historic storefronts and civic buildings in a downtown area so small businesses can reopen and heritage corridors remain intact. Neighborhood and site‑wide efforts: Coordinating repairs across multiple historic resources within a district or campus—including hazard abatement, structural fixes, and weatherproofing—to restore public access.

4) Capacity to manage recovery - Compliance reviews and permitting support: Funding staff time to process preservation reviews required by law, helping communities move disaster‑recovery projects forward quickly and responsibly. Survey and inventory of damaged areas: Field teams document storm‑, flood‑, and fire‑impacted historic resources; results feed public databases and guide repair and mitigation. Register activities and documentation: Preparing nominations and formal records for significant places affected by disasters, strengthening recognition and long‑term protection.

financialInformation.additionalInformation: Funding is based on Congressional actions wherein appropriations are made after natural disasters.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description: Provide Notice of Funding Opportunity and outreach for the award of $48 million in Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund (ESHPF) funding to be obligated in FY2026.

1) Planning and Assessments - Funding provides critical support for communities in the immediate aftermath of disasters by funding thorough assessments and preservation planning. Specialists examine damaged historic buildings, cultural sites, and public landmarks to understand the extent of harm and identify urgent stabilization needs. These assessments lead directly to carefully developed preservation plans that include scopes of work, cost estimates, and repair strategies. By investing in planning up front, communities are better equipped to protect historic resources, prevent further deterioration, and move more quickly toward safe reopening.

2) Emergency Stabilization and Repairs - Once damage is documented, funding helps stabilize and repair historic places so they remain safe and usable. This can include reinforcing weakened roofs and foundations, repairing structural components, addressing water intrusion, or restoring features that were damaged by wind, fire, or flooding. This work saves meaningful community landmarks—from historic hospitals and theaters to long‑standing hotels and religious buildings—allowing them to continue hosting programs, providing services, and anchoring local identity. Repairs also extend to historically significant infrastructure, such as railroad equipment, ensuring that hands‑on pieces of local history remain accessible for future generations.

3) District‑Wide Recovery - In many areas, a disaster affects not just a single building but entire historic districts. Funding supports coordinated, district‑wide recovery efforts that help multiple cultural properties at once. Stabilization and repair across commercial corridors allow small businesses housed in historic storefronts to reopen more quickly. Rehabilitating civic buildings and public spaces preserves the character of historic downtowns and strengthens local tourism and revitalization efforts. These comprehensive recovery projects ensure that entire communities can regain their sense of place after devastating storms, floods, or fires.

4) Capacity Building and Preservation Services - Funding strengthens the ability of states, Tribes, territories, nonprofits, and educational institutions to manage disaster‑related preservation needs. Funding helps organizations complete legally required preservation reviews, maintain updated inventories of storm‑damaged resources, and prepare documentation like National Register nominations. Many awards support training, technical assistance, and disaster planning so that local stewards know how to respond effectively when future emergencies occur. Others improve digital systems and databases used for compliance, which speeds up recovery projects and enhances transparency. These services ensure that preservation work is done responsibly, efficiently, and with long‑term resilience in mind.

description: Credentials for these programs are outlined in the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.), 36 CFR 61, the Historic Preservation Fund Grants Manual, 2 CFR 200 in its entirety, and appropriations law as enacted by Congress. In general, sites eligible for these programs must be listed in, or eligible for listing in, the National Register of Historic places.

They may include: State Historic Preservation Offices in the 50 states, 5 territories, 3 Freely Associated States, and District of Columbia (SHPOs); States; Tribal governments with signed Memorandum of Agreements with the National Park Service to assume the duties of the State Historic Preservation Office on Tribal lands, as defined in 54 USC 3001 et seq. (THPOs); Federally-recognized Tribes, Alaska Native Villages/Corporations, and Native Hawaiian Organizations as defined by 54 USC § 300309, 54 USC 300313 and 54 USC 300314 (Tribes); local governments (including Certified Local Governments); and/or nonprofits. Some programs may not be open to all of these entities, dependent on Congressional intent.

Eligible projects must be for sites listed in or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, or similar Tribal register, and must be located within areas receiving FEMA major disaster declarations under the Stafford Act. assistanceUsage.description: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund (ESHPF) grants must be used to preserve historic and cultural resources located in areas that have received major disaster declarations and are listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or similar Tribal register. Grants assist in physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administration activities necessary to carry out the preceding activities. All funded projects must follow the applicable Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. In accordance with 54 USC 302902, grantees must agree to assume, after completion of a rehabilitation project, the cost of the continued maintenance, repair, and administration of the property in a manner satisfactory to the Secretary of the Interior. Restrictions on the use of funding are set by Congress and the parameters of the specific supplemental appropriation as well as in the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.), 36 CFR 61, the Historic Preservation Fund Grants Manual, and 2 CFR 200. Acquisition, local government certification, and tax incentives are not eligible activities. Project work must comply with what is popularly referred to as Section 106 (54 USC 306108) and Section 110 (54 USC 306107) of the National Historic Preservation Act as well as the National Environmental Policy Act (PL 91-190).

overview.objective: To preserve the cultural resources of the Route 66 corridor and to authorize the Secretary of the Interior to provide assistance. The program provides cost-share grants to help preserve the most significant and representative historic sites related to the route’s period of significance (1926-1985), and cooperative agreements for study, planning, preservation, rehabilitation, and restoration related to the Route 66 corridor.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Route 66 Corridor Preservation Program supports the preservation and public understanding of the historic resources that define U.S. Route 66, one of America’s most recognizable highways. Authorized by Public Law 106‑45 and administered by the National Park Service, the program provides financial and technical assistance to help ensure that the cultural, historic, and educational assets of the Route 66 corridor remain available for future generations. The program’s purpose is to identify, protect, and enhance the most significant buildings, structures, road segments, and cultural landscapes associated with Route 66’s period of national importance (1926–1985). Through cost‑share grants, cooperative agreements, and preservation guidance, the program supports projects that restore historic properties, strengthen community stewardship, document important stories, and create educational materials that expand public awareness of Route 66’s role in American history.

list.description:
1) Historic Preservation and Cultural Heritage - Funding supports the preservation of historically significant sites, including: restoring architectural features of historic buildings such as windows, roofs, and signage, rehabilitating infrastructure like plumbing, electrical systems, and structural elements to maintain historical integrity, and revitalizing old service stations, motels, and other roadside landmarks.

2) Educational Outreach and Public Engagement - Funding supports the creation of educational materials and programs that develop multimedia content such as short films, story maps, and lesson plans aligned with academic standards, and engage students and the general public in learning about cultural and historical themes through accessible, classroom-friendly resources.

3) Infrastructure and Site Rehabilitation - funding supports the repair and restoration of key features of historic corridors, including buildings and landscapes, improving visitor access and safety while maintaining historical authenticity.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding.  Program anticipates funding projects that provide cost-share grants to help preserve the most significant and representative historic sites related to the route’s period of significance (1926-1985), and cooperative agreements for study, planning, preservation, rehabilitation, and restoration related to the Route 66 corridor.

list.description:

2) Bringing New Life to a Landmark Building: A historic information bureau building is undergoing repairs to its windows, roof, plumbing, and more—ensuring it remains a vibrant part of the community and a destination for travelers.

3) Interactive Learning for Students: Educational video modules are being created for middle and high school students. These lessons explore the history of Route 66 and its impact on communities, businesses, and culture—making history come alive in classrooms.

4) Strengthening National Partnerships: Funding supports the development of a nonprofit organization that brings together people from all eight Route 66 states. This group leads efforts to preserve, promote, and celebrate the highway’s legacy.

overview.objective: The objectives of this program are to assist, advise, and cooperate with States or their political subdivisions, landowners, private organizations, other federal agencies or authorized wild and scenic river management councils or committees to plan, protect, and manage river resources associated with those rivers designated into the National Wild and Scenic River system for which the Department of the Interior is authorized to act as the federal administrator.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
This program supports locally led efforts to protect and enhance nationally significant river corridors. These rivers possess exceptional natural, cultural, historical, and recreational values, and the program strengthens community-based stewardship that ensures these resources are preserved for current and future generations.
Through cooperative agreements, local organizations, community partners, and government agencies work together to carry out the goals identified in river management plans developed with broad public involvement. These plans provide a shared framework for conservation, recreation, science, education, and cultural preservation.
Funded projects have helped communities safeguard ecological values by monitoring water quality, restoring habitats, removing debris, improving streambanks, managing invasive species, and conducting scientific studies that support long-term stewardship. Local partners also maintain and enhance public access by improving trails, recreation sites, and river entry points, ensuring visitors can enjoy safe outdoor experiences.

list.description:
1) Protecting Wild and Scenic Rivers - Funding supports the implementation of river management plans that preserve the natural, cultural, and recreational values of designated wild and scenic rivers. This includes monitoring local land use, reviewing ordinances, and ensuring compliance with conservation goals.

2) Supporting Local and Regional Partnerships - Funding enables collaboration between nonprofit organizations, local governments, and federal agencies to manage river corridors. These partnerships help coordinate planning, enforcement, and public engagement efforts.

3) Advancing Conservation and Public Access - Projects include land protection, invasive species management, historical site surveys, and improvements to river access points. These efforts enhance ecological health, preserve heritage, and expand recreational opportunities for the public.

Communities and partner organizations are working together to protect a nationally significant river corridor, preserving its natural scenery, wildlife habitat, and public access so future generations can continue to enjoy and explore the river.

Local committees are implementing river management plans that safeguard ecological, scenic, and recreational values. This includes reviewing development proposals and community plans to ensure growth aligns with long‑term conservation goals.

Historic buildings, cultural sites, and river‑related landmarks are being identified, documented, and protected. These efforts help preserve the region’s heritage and make its stories accessible to visitors and residents.


Habitat restoration projects are improving conditions for fish, birds, and other wildlife. Activities include invasive species removal, native plant restoration, streambank stabilization, and ongoing scientific monitoring of sensitive species.

Community groups and volunteers are enhancing recreation opportunities by maintaining riverside trails, improving access points, and providing educational signs and materials that help the public enjoy the river safely and responsibly.

Local organizations are awarding small community grants that support land stewardship, environmental education, historical research, and public outreach projects. These initiatives strengthen community involvement in caring for the river’s natural and cultural resources.

list.description:
1) Protecting the Wild and Scenic Delaware River: Funding is helping local organizations and communities work together to protect one of the nation’s most treasured river corridors. These efforts are preserving natural beauty, cultural heritage, and public access for generations to come.

2) Safeguarding River Values - Funding supports the implementation of river management plans that protect the ecological, scenic, and recreational values of the river. This includes reviewing local development plans and ordinances to ensure they align with conservation goals.

3) Preserving History and Culture - funding helps identify and protect historic buildings, sites, and landscapes along the river. These efforts ensure that the region’s rich cultural heritage is honored and shared with the public.

In FY 2026, communities and partner organizations worked together to protect nationally significant river corridors, preserving natural scenery, wildlife habitat, and public access so future generations can continue to enjoy and explore these rivers.
Local committees implemented river management plans that safeguarded ecological, scenic, and recreational values. Their work included reviewing development proposals and community plans to ensure that growth aligned with long‑term conservation goals and supported the protection of free‑flowing river conditions.
Historic buildings, cultural landscapes, and river‑related heritage sites were identified, documented, and protected, ensuring that important cultural stories and resources along river corridors were preserved and shared with the public.
Habitat restoration projects improved conditions for fish, birds, and other wildlife through invasive species removal, native plant restoration, streambank stabilization, and scientific monitoring of sensitive species. These efforts strengthened river ecosystems and supported long-term environmental health.
Community groups and volunteers enhanced river‑related recreation by maintaining trails, improving access points, and creating educational signs and materials that help visitors enjoy the outdoors safely and responsibly while learning more about their local river environments.
Local organizations awarded small community grants supporting land stewardship, environmental education, historical research, and public outreach projects, increasing community involvement and advancing the long-term protection of natural, cultural, and recreational river values.

overview.objective: The Southwest Border Resource Protection Program provides financial assistance to educational institutions, nonprofit organizations, tribes, and local and state agencies to improve resource stewardship, achieve international cooperation, provide meaningful interpretation and conduct scientific research, which will lead to increased appreciation and understanding of our shared natural and cultural heritage along our international border with Mexico.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Southwest Border Resource Protection Program helps communities, tribes, educators, and organizations safeguard the unique natural and cultural heritage found along the United States–Mexico border. Through financial assistance, the program supports projects that strengthen resource stewardship, expand environmental and cultural understanding, improve public interpretation, and promote collaborative scientific research.
This program serves educational institutions, nonprofit organizations, tribal governments, and local and state agencies who work to protect and interpret shared cross‑border resources. What makes this program unique is its focus on cooperation and on preserving landscapes, wildlife, historic sites, and cultural connections that span both sides of the border. By encouraging collaboration across communities and disciplines, the program helps deepen public appreciation of the diverse, interconnected heritage of this border region.

list.description:
1) Wildlife Corridor Assessment - Funds are used to monitor wildlife movement across border infrastructure, evaluate crossing structures, and engage students in conservation internships.

2) Rare Plant Conservation - Funds are allocated to study a rare orchid species that remains underground most of the year. The research includes habitat assessment and aims to inform fire management strategies.

3) Riparian Habitat Monitoring - Funding expands a beaver monitoring program along a river basin to assess habitat suitability and promote riparian conservation through community involvement and educational outreach.

4) Migratory Bird Research - Funding supports tracking of a vulnerable bird species using satellite tags, genetic analysis, and habitat restoration. The project also includes public outreach and STEM education.

5) Water Resource and Wildlife Interaction Study - Research focuses on natural rock basins that collect water. The study quantifies water availability, wildlife usage, and predicts animal movement patterns in response to water scarcity.

Projects monitor wildlife to understand population trends, habitat conditions, and how environmental changes affect species over time. These efforts gather information on animal movement, diet, and ecosystem needs, helping communities and scientists make informed conservation decisions.

Studies analyze water from rivers, springs, and groundwater to understand water chemistry, identify pollution concerns, locate the sources of important springs, and guide long‑term water management. This work supports community efforts to protect sensitive water supplies.

Restoration activities improve damaged or sensitive environments by planting native vegetation, enhancing soil and water conditions, repairing erosion, and stabilizing streambanks. These actions strengthen ecosystems, support wildlife habitat, and improve landscape resilience.

Trainings and workshops help residents, landowners, and local organizations learn how to monitor natural resources, restore habitats, and collect scientific data. Building these skills encourages active community participation in environmental stewardship.

Creation of bilingual educational materials, such as videos, brochures, maps, or social media content, helps the public learn about local wildlife, water resources, and cultural traditions. Clear, accessible information encourages broader community engagement.

Scientific data collection using tools like genetic sampling, camera traps, and water‑monitoring sensors fills knowledge gaps about species, habitats, and environmental changes. This information supports effective conservation planning and resource management.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Saving Rare and Vulnerable Wildlife - Scientists are using satellite tags to follow the migration of a unique desert bird. They're also studying its feathers to understand pollution exposure and working to protect its nesting areas from invasive plants.

2) Restoring Native Plants and Habitats - Conservationists are collecting seeds from native plants that support bees and butterflies. These seeds are used to restore damaged landscapes and support biodiversity.

3) Studying Water and Wildlife Connections - Researchers are studying natural rock basins that hold rainwater. These tiny pools are lifelines for animals in dry areas. The project helps predict how wildlife will adapt to changing water availability.

The Southwest Border Protection program advanced scientific research, conservation, and cross‑border collaboration to protect shared natural and cultural resources. Partners worked together to study wildlife, monitor water quality, restore sensitive habitats, and expand community engagement.
A major accomplishment was a multi‑day symposium that connected scientists, land managers, and community leaders to share research, discuss challenges, and identify solutions. The event featured field learning, workshops, public presentations, and bilingual interpretation to support broad participation and long‑term partnerships.
Across the region, researchers collected new wildlife and water‑resource data, using tools such as genetic sampling, cameras, and hydrologic monitoring, to improve understanding of species trends, habitat needs, and water quality. Community‑led conservation projects provided training, volunteer opportunities, and restoration activities that helped residents care for riparian areas, wildlife habitats, and culturally important landscapes. Bilingual outreach and accessible educational materials strengthened public awareness and connection to shared natural and cultural heritage.

Thousands of miles of unauthorized roads and trails have been created, major ecological processes and the migration patterns of wildlife have been disrupted, important historic sites have been vandalized, and archaeological sites have been looted. title: Historic Preservation Fund Grants-in-Aid for Competitive Grants

overview.objective:
The objectives of the competitive grant programs under this Assistance Listing are broad but are all generally intended to provide funding to document and preserve cultural resources that are important to American history. Following Congressional guidance, specific grant programs emphasize social, cultural, or historic themes and target funding to historic events like the struggle for civil and equal rights in the United States, documenting and preserving the stories of underrepresented communities, or preserving sites associated with the founding of the nation.

Examples of grant programs could include: African American Civil Rights, Paul Bruhn Historic Revitalization, History of Equal Rights, Semiquincentennial, Underrepresented Communities, Tribal Heritage, and future competitive grant programs as may be created by Congress.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports competitive grants from the National Park Service’s Historic Preservation Fund to help communities protect significant places, stories, and cultural resources tied to American history. These grants fund activities such as documenting historic sites, preparing National Register nominations, developing preservation plans, and carrying out physical preservation work. Eligible applicants include state and local governments, federally recognized Tribes and Native organizations, nonprofit organizations, and educational institutions. Competitive grant programs also focus on specific themes—such as African American civil rights, underrepresented communities, Tribal heritage, and the nation’s founding—allowing applicants to pursue funding aligned with distinct preservation goals.

list.description:
1) Building Repairs and Structural Preservation - Grants are used to fix leaking roofs, crumbling chimneys, and damaged brickwork on historic buildings to prevent further deterioration; and the repair or replacement of original windows and doors to maintain historical accuracy while improving energy efficiency and safety.

2) System and Safety Upgrades - Projects include fire safety improvements including installing fire alarms, sprinkler systems, and emergency exits to meet modern safety codes; and accessibility enhancements including adding ramps, elevators, or accessible restrooms to ensure historic sites are inclusive and ADA-compliant.

3) Historic and Cultural Site Restoration - Funding is used to restore original finishes like plaster walls, wood floors, and decorative ceilings in historic interiors. Projects often focus on revitalizing historic educational or civic buildings for continued community use.

4) Documentation and Planning - Grants fund detailed assessments of historic buildings to guide future preservation work. Some projects aim to document and nominate properties for inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding grant programs that include African American Civil Rights, Paul Bruhn Historic Revitalization, History of Equal Rights, Semiquincentennial,  and Underrepresented Communities Grants.

awardRecipientBasis.name: Discretionary and Competitive Recipient Selection Award

list.description:
1) Saving Historic Buildings - Funding has helped restore and protect dozens of historic buildings that tell the story of our communities. These efforts include: repairing roofs, chimneys, and foundations to prevent water damage and structural collapse; restoring original windows, doors, and decorative features to maintain the character and authenticity of historic sites; and rehabilitating interiors—from wood floors to ornate ceilings—so these spaces can continue to serve the public.

2) Modernizing for Safety and Access - Many historic buildings were not built with modern needs in mind. Grants have enabled: fire safety upgrades, including alarms and sprinkler systems; accessibility improvements, such as ramps and ADA-compliant restrooms; and new HVAC and electrical systems to make buildings more energy-efficient and comfortable year-round.

3) Reviving Cultural Landmarks - Theaters, museums, and community centers have received funding to: restore performance spaces and public gathering areas; preserve historic churches and schools that have long served as cultural and educational anchors; and reopen historic venues that had fallen into disrepair, bringing them back to life for concerts, exhibits, and community events.

4) Protecting History Through Documentation - Grants have supported: historic structure reports and preservation plans that guide long-term care; National Register nominations to formally recognize important sites; and research and documentation of underrepresented histories.

title: National Wildland Fire Management and Natural Resource Training and Workforce Development

overview.objective: The goal of this listing is to provide financial assistance to reduce and mitigate the risk of catastrophic wildland fires on federal land and/or adjacent non-federal land and communities and their natural resources. This will be accomplished through response, rehabilitation, assessment, planning, implementation, monitoring, treatment, and maintenance of hazardous fuels reduction and other wildland fire management activities. Financial assistance will provide for a training and workforce development program with an emphasis on wildland fire management and natural resources skills.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This listing provides for financial assistance to develop skills and training for those with little or no experience in wildland fire and natural resource management.

list.description:
1.) Training the Next Generation of Wildland Fire Professionals: Programs that recruit and train young adults for careers in wildland fire management. Participants gain hands‑on experience through activities such as clearing brush, maintaining trails, and learning how fire crews prepare for and respond to wildfires. These programs help build a skilled workforce while reducing hazardous vegetation that can fuel dangerous fires.

2.) Reducing Fire Hazards Near Public Lands and Communities: Assistance may be used to thin dense vegetation, remove dead trees, or conduct other fuel‑reduction projects that lower the chances of severe wildfires. These efforts help protect nearby homes, infrastructure, natural resources, and recreation areas by creating safer conditions and strategic zones where firefighters can more effectively stop advancing fires.

3.) Restoring Lands After Wildfires:  Teams that repair damage caused by wildfires, such as stabilizing slopes, planting native vegetation, removing hazards, or repairing trails and access routes. Restoring burned areas helps prevent erosion, protect waterways, and make the land safer and more accessible for the public.

Program has not yet selected projects for funding. Program anticipates funding projects that provide financial assistance to reduce and mitigate the risk of catastrophic wildland fires on federal land and/or adjacent non-federal land and communities and their natural resources, and provide training and workforce development to its participants.

overview.objective: Through a multidisciplinary collaborative program, identify and provide information and funding needed to sustain subsistence fisheries and wildlife management on public lands for rural Alaskans. The program includes maintaining sound management principles and conservation of healthy populations of fish and wildlife and other renewable resources.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: This program supports the collaborative stewardship of fish and wildlife that rural Alaskans rely on for subsistence. Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) created an enduring legacy of national public lands in Alaska for the American people. Title II of ANILCA designated 10 new park areas and expanded three existing units. Congress respected the importance of these lands to Alaska rural residents and provided for traditional subsistence activities in nine of the new ANILCA park areas and two of the expanded areas. Four of the ANILCA park units—Bering Land Bridge National Preserve, Cape Krusenstern National Monument, Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve and Kobuk Valley National Park—have purpose statements that include protecting subsistence resources as a specific park function. In addition, Congress established a priority in Title VIII that gives local rural residents precedence for using fish or wildlife resources. This is commonly known as the "rural preference" and grants subsistence uses priority over other uses, such as non-local sport hunting and fishing.

list.description:
A partner organization coordinated community meetings where subsistence users shared observations on changing conditions and resource needs. The sessions helped document seasonal trends in wildlife and supported updates to management recommendations.

A regional association organized travel for community representatives to attend advisory commission meetings. Their participation ensured that local knowledge and subsistence perspectives were incorporated into discussions on regulatory proposals.

A fisheries group conducted in-season monitoring of salmon runs by interviewing harvesters and compiling catch observations. The survey results informed timely management actions and helped balance conservation goals with community harvest needs.

overview.objective: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement and plan forest, rangeland, and watershed restoration projects by facilitating partnerships with authorized states, counties, and federally recognized Indian tribes. The GNA authority specifically allows the National Park Service (NPS) to enhance state-federal relationships and address cross-boundary land restoration needs. This includes activities such as treating insect-and-disease-infested trees; reducing hazardous fuels; and any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat. This type of work reduces wildfire risk to habitat, communities, and state trust lands; creates greater forest and watershed resilience against drought, insects, disease, and wildfire; and expands much-needed work across state and federal lands.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) for Restoration Program helps state, local, and tribal governments partner with the National Park Service to restore and protect healthy forests, rangelands, and watersheds. Projects funded under 16 USC 2113a may include restoration and management activities. Projects range from treating noxious weeds and invasive species across multiple ownerships to fuels management activities like thinning, prescribed burning, and other treatments to reduce wildfire risk and improve forest resiliency. GNA can also support community assistance projects that benefit multiple landowners, such as thinning around communities at risk, and forest management activities aimed at increasing resilience to wildfire, insects, disease, and drought. Rangeland plant restoration, whether necessitated by wildfire, drought, or invasive species, including seed collection and planting, is also eligible. While NPS decision-making cannot be delegated, cooperating entities can assist with NEPA documentation. Finally, riparian restoration projects, including erosion control and revegetation, are often more effective when implemented across entire stream reaches and are therefore well-suited for GNA partnerships.

assistanceUsage.description:
Projects are primarily conducted on federal lands administered by the NPS located in the Western United States and Alaska. Projects may also be conducted on other lands to enhance state or Indian Tribe-federal relationships addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include activities confined to Authorized Restoration Service which are activities to treat insect and disease-infected trees, activities to reduce hazardous fuels, and any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat. The National Park Service must provide or approve silviculture prescriptions and marking guidelines to be applied to public lands in timber sale projects. The term “Federal land” does not include a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System; Federal land on which the removal of vegetation is prohibited or restricted by Act of Congress or Presidential proclamation (including the applicable implementation plan); or a wilderness study area. Does not include construction, reconstruction, repair, or restoration of paved or permanent roads or parking areas, other than the reconstruction, repair, or restoration of a road that is necessary to carry out authorized restoration services pursuant to a good neighbor agreement. Does not include construction, alteration, repair or replacement of public buildings or works. NPS’s funding is discretionary.
Noxious weeds and invasive species treatments: Treatment of noxious weeds and invasive species is often carried out across multiple ownerships in a coordinated effort. GNA can be an effective tool to partner with a cooperating entity that is carrying out weed treatments, whether using herbicide, mechanical, or biological controls, in a coordinated cross-boundary effort. 
Fuels Management: Mechanical treatments (e.g., thinning, piling, mastication, mowing), chemical and biological applications, and prescribed fire to protect communities at risk, improve wildfire resiliency, and provide a safe and effective wildfire response.
Community Assistance: Projects across ownership boundaries with mutual benefit and the ability to leverage funds to complete work on the ground. Some treatments could include thinning around a community at risk, juniper removal to improve landscape resiliency.
Forest Management: Conduct treatments to enhance the resilience of forests to wildfire, insect, disease, and drought through density management.
Rangeland plant restoration: Whether impacts are from wildfire, drought, or noxious weeds and invasive species, it is often necessary to aid the re-establishment of rangeland vegetation. This could entail development of plant materials, seed collection, site preparation, and seed or seedling planting. Native plant restoration is also often a cross-boundary need, and where a cooperating entity is conducting these activities, GNA can be used to conduct these activities on National Park Service (NPS) managed lands.
Wildlife movement, migration, and habitat connectivity: GNA can be used to facilitate cross-boundary cooperative habitat restoration and rangeland structural improvements to improve habitat connectivity and support unimpeded movement of wildlife populations across landscapes. Examples of cooperative habitat connectivity projects may include: cross-boundary work associated with fence removals or upgrades to reduce animal fatalities and movement barriers; invasive species control and reseeding or planting of native vegetation along migration corridors and stopover areas; and enhancement of water resource availability within important wildlife movement areas (i.e., development and protection of natural springs, removal of invasive riparian species to increase water availability, construction of guzzlers and other artificial water sources, wet meadow restoration, etc.).

overview.objective:
The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement recreation enhancement or improvement services: The term "recreation enhancement or improvement services" means- (A) establishing, repairing, restoring, improving, relocating, constructing, or reconstructing new or existing- (i) trails or trailheads; (ii) campgrounds and camping areas; (iii) cabins; (iv) picnic areas or other day use areas; (v) shooting ranges; (vi) restroom or shower facilities; (vii) paved or permanent roads or parking areas that serve existing recreation facilities or areas; (viii) fishing piers, wildlife viewing platforms, docks, or other constructed features at a recreation site; (ix) boat landings; (x) hunting or fishing sites; (xi) infrastructure within ski areas; or
(xii) visitor centers or other interpretative sites; and (B) activities that create, improve, or restore access to existing recreation facilities or areas.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Projects funded under 16 USC 8571 (Good Neighbor Authority) may include working with State, local, or tribal governments to enhance recreation and improve visitor recreational access. It funds projects like trail building or repair, campground upgrades, restroom improvements, and picnic area expansions. These projects can happen on federal land—or on nearby tribal or local lands—to create seamless recreation areas for everyone to enjoy.

list.description:

This road is the only two‑way access to popular recreation spots including campgrounds, cemeteries, stream access points, and multiple trailheads. By restoring the road to pre‑storm conditions, the program ensured that families, visitors, and community members could once again travel safely to these valued outdoor areas.

2) Rebuilding a Coastal Recreation Corridor - Another project rebuilt a storm‑damaged segment of a coastal roadway serving campgrounds, picnic areas, and trailheads. The reconstruction restored essential public access and strengthened the road so it can better withstand future coastal storms. This work supports year‑round recreation and helps sustain the local economies that rely on tourism and outdoor activities.

overview.objective: To assist State and local governments, and certain eligible (501(c)(3) tax-exempt status) non-profit organizations with acquiring surplus Federal real property for various public uses that benefit communities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: Based on a determination by GSA of a property’s highest and best use, surplus Federal real and related personal property may be conveyed to State and local governments and, in some cases, certain eligible non-profit organizations for various public purposes or uses as allowed by law. These conveyances are called Public Benefit Conveyances (PBCs). Under the law, PBCs are completed without monetary consideration or at discounts of up to 100 percent of the fair market value; and, depending on the PBC, the use of the property is restricted for a period of up to 30 years or in perpetuity. Property may be conveyed at a discount of up to 100 percent for Homeless assistance use; if the property is conveyed by deed, it must be used for homeless assistance purposes for 30 years; if it is conveyed by lease or permit the property must be used for a period according to the terms of the lease or permit, which is generally not less than one year. Surplus Federal real property is also conveyed at discounts of up to 100 percent for public park or recreation use (restriction: perpetuity); public health or educational purposes (restriction: 30 years for both); historic monument (restriction: perpetuity); correctional (restriction: perpetuity); law enforcement (restriction: perpetuity); emergency management response use, including fire and rescue services (restriction: perpetuity); self-help housing (restriction: 30 years); port facility use (restriction: perpetuity), wildlife conservation (restriction: perpetuity); public airport (restriction: perpetuity) and public highway use (restriction: none): public airport use (restriction: perpetuity); wildlife conservation (restriction: perpetuity).

awardProcedure.description: NEH staff review all applications for eligibility, completeness, and responsiveness. Peer reviewers are experts in their fields with knowledge and expertise relevant to the activities that the program supports. NEH instructs peer reviewers to evaluate applications according to established review criteria. Peer reviewers must comply with federal ethics rules governing conflicts of interest. NEH program officers supplement the peer reviewers’ comments to address matters of fact or significant points that the peer reviewers have overlooked. They then make funding recommendations to the National Council on the Humanities and the NEH Chairman. The National Council meets at least twice each year to review applications and advise the NEH Chairman. By law, the Chair has the sole authority to make final funding decisions.

description:
Applicants are required to complete the SF-424 - Application for Federal Assistance and attach the following supporting documents.
	1.  Project Abstract:  In approximately 500 words or less, provide a brief abstract of the proposed project. As applicable, include other information relevant to an understanding of the overall project.
	2.  Project plan:  In approximately 500 words or less, the applicant must include a detailed timeline for the tasks outlined in the project description and proposed milestones.

This may include evidence of past experience with projects similar in scope as defined by the NOFO, to include descriptions of the engagement model, examples of successful leadership and management of a project of similar scale and budget (or greater), or related work in this field.
 	4.  Proposed Budget:  In approximately 500 words or less, the proposed budget should identify all costs and proposed expenditures, to additional compensation and honoraria (and to whom); equipment costs; production costs; and travel costs.

overview.objective: Title XI, Section 71101 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA or The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law or (BIL)), Public Law 117-58 amended section 741 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C. 16091) to authorize the EPA’S Clean School Bus (CSB) Program to award grants, contracts, and rebates for the replacement of existing school buses with clean school buses. IIJA appropriates $ 5 billion for the program over five Federal fiscal years (FY 22-26). The objective of this assistance is, to the maximum extent practicable, achieve nationwide deployment of clean school buses and zero-emission school buses and to ensure a broad geographic distribution of awards. The CSB Program will fund the replacement of existing school buses with cleaner buses that result in better air quality on the bus, in bus loading areas, and throughout the communities in which they operate. The Clean School Bus Program works to reduce pollution emitted from existing school buses by replacing them with cleaner school buses. Priority is given to projects which propose to replace buses that serve high-need local education agencies; rural school districts; Bureau of Indian Affairs-funded school districts; and school districts receiving basic support payments for children who reside on Indian land.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: School buses in the United States travel more than 4 billion miles each year, providing the safest transportation to and from school for more than 25 million American children every day. list.description: Projects include the replacement of diesel and non-diesel internal combustion engine school buses with battery electric, compressed natural gas (CNG), or propane drivetrain school buses, along with the installation of the associated charging infrastructure for electric school buses. Eligible vehicles include Class 3 – 7+ school buses, and eligible charging infrastructure includes installation between the electrical meter and charging port, such as charging equipment, design and engineering, installation costs, and related intelligent equipment or software designed to monitor bus and infrastructure performance.

overview.objective: Provides technical and financial assistance to State of New Mexico Environment Department and the Regents of New Mexico State University/Carlsbad Environmental Monitoring and Research Center (NMSU/CEMRC) for the conduct of projects/activities to support DOE's and the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) mission and to provide the public assurances that implemented DOE programs are protective of human health and the environment. The purpose of the WIPP Environmental Monitoring Project is to establish and maintain independent environmental research and monitoring in the vicinity of the WIPP and to make the results easily accessible to all interested parties. This project began implementation during the WIPP pre-disposal phase, and is continuing during the operational (disposal) phase. The environmental monitoring projects are organized and carried out independent of direct oversight by Department Of Energy (DOE). Analytical results and interpretations from the monitoring are published by NMSU/CEMRC to inform the public and particularly the environmental science community.  The State of New Mexico holds the permit for disposal of Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) waste at WIPP and the independent monitoring provides assurance to the State that WIPP is operating in accordance with its RCRA Permit.

title: Office of Science Financial Assistance Program

overview.objective:
SC is the Nation’s largest Federal sponsor of basic research in the physical sciences and the lead Federal agency supporting fundamental scientific research for our Nation’s energy future. SC is an established leader of the U.S. scientific discovery and innovation enterprise.

Over the decades, SC investments and accomplishments in basic research and enabling research capabilities have provided the foundations for new technologies, businesses, and industries, making significant contributions to our nation’s economy, national security, and quality of life.  Additional descriptions of recent science discoveries can
be found at https://science.osti.gov/Science-Features/Science-Highlights.

SC accomplishes its mission and advances national goals by supporting:
- Science for energy, economic and national security―building a foundation of scientific and technical knowledge to spur discoveries and innovations for advancing the Department’s mission. SC supports a wide range of funding modalities from single principal investigators to large team-based activities to engage in fundamental research on energy production, conversion, storage, transmission, and use, and on our understanding of the earth systems.
- The frontiers of science—exploring nature’s mysteries from the study of fundamental subatomic particles, atoms, and molecules that are the building blocks of the materials of our universe and everything in it to the DNA, proteins, and cells that are the building blocks of life. Each of the programs in SC supports research probing the most fundamental disciplinary questions.
- The 21st Century tools of science—providing the nation’s researchers with 28 state-of-the-art national scientific user
facilities, the most advanced tools of modern science, propelling the U.S. to the forefront of science, technology
development, and deployment through innovation.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: SC’s basic research portfolio, which includes extramural grants and contracts supporting nearly 29,000 researchers located at over 300 institutions and the 17 DOE national laboratories, spanning all fifty states and the District of Columbia. Our researchers advance our understanding of the natural universe and create the discoveries that can be exploited in numerous fields.

overview.objective: (1) To grow the U.S. scientific community through university involvement in areas of fundamental science and technology relevant to stockpile stewardship; (2) to promote and sustain scientific interactions between the academic community and scientists at the NNSA laboratories; (3) to train scientists in specific areas of long-term research relevant to stockpile stewardship; (4) to increase the availability of unique experimental facilities sited at NNSA's laboratories to the academic community, particularly for collaborations in areas of relevance to stockpile stewardship; and (5) to develop and maintain a long-term recruiting pipeline to NNSA's laboratories by increasing the visibility of NNSA's Defense Program's scientific activities to the U.S. faculty and student communities.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Nation’s nuclear weapons stockpile is a vital part
of our national security infrastructure. Ensuring that this
deterrent is second to none requires the best science and technology. Having top tier scientists and engineers in the areas critical to stockpile stewardship is the only
way to ensure the best science and technology. The National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA)
supports this effort through the Office of Defense  Programs.

list.description: Funding may be used to fund grants or cooperative agreements to conduct fundamental science and technology research of relevance to stockpile stewardship. overview.objective: The objective of this cooperative agreement is to strengthen public safety and security by providing supplementary financial support to the County of Nye, Nye County Sheriff’s Office.  This financial support is intended to increase operational capacity and enhance the law enforcement presence at and surrounding the Nevada National Security Sites (NNSS) in Nye County, Nevada.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: The County of Nye, Nye County Sheriff’s Office fulfills a vital public role by delivering comprehensive law enforcement services, including both civil and criminal enforcement, oversight, control and containment of public protests and demonstrations, and detention of individuals suspected of violations of Federal law until transfer to the appropriate Federal agency in the County of Nye.  Situated in the southeastern part of Nye County, the NNSS is located approximately 65 miles northwest of the City of Las Vegas.  Maintaining a law enforcement presence near the NNSS improves public safety and security.

list.description: Calendar year 2025 Actuals:  $393,000.

The cooperative agreement will enhance the County of Nye, Nye County Sheriff's Office to provide the following support at or near the NNSS:
•	Control and contain public protests and demonstrations. 
•	Conduct periodic traffic enforcement operations to maintain roadway safety.
•	Support the NNSS contractor protective force response with trespassers and protestors including lawful detention, citation, arrest and transportation of arrested individuals.
•	Investigate and collect evidence of suspected civil and criminal acts within the boundaries of the NNSS.
•	Assist emergency response personnel in responding to emergencies at and near the NNSS located in Nye County, Nevada.

Calendar Year 2027 Projections:  $551,132 maximum reimbursement ceiling for law enforcement services.

overview.objective:
The purpose of the Transparency in Coverage Enforcement Grant is to provide funding to states to strengthen the implementation and enforcement of the Transparency in Coverage (TiC) requirements authorized under Part A of title XXVII of the Public Health Service Act, including section 2715A (Provision of Additional Information). The grant is intended to enhance state oversight of health insurance issuers by building state capacity to monitor issuer compliance with the TiC requirements, investigate potential violations, and support enforcement activities that improve consumers' access to accurate, meaningful, and timely health care pricing information, including through internet-based price comparison tools and machine-readable files.

Grant funding may be used to support activities such as developing consumer education and outreach materials, testing and validating internet-based price comparison tools and machine-readable files, training staff on the technical aspects of the TiC requirements, developing compliance review and enforcement methodologies, and supporting complaint intake and investigations.
overview.assistanceListingDescription:
The Transparency in Coverage Enforcement Grant will provide funding to states to strengthen their implementation and enforcement of the Transparency in Coverage (TiC) requirements under Part A of title XXVII of the Public Health Service Act. Grant funds will supports activities that enhance state oversight of health insurance issuers, improve compliance with TiC requirements, and increase consumers' access to meaningful health care pricing information.

The grant is open to all 50 states and the District of Columbia. This grant is intended for the state agency responsible for regulating health insurance issuers and enforcing the applicable federal health insurance requirements under Part A of title XXVII of the Public Health Service Act. Grant funding may be used to strengthen enforcement capacity through activities such as consumer education and outreach, staff training, compliance and enforcement initiatives, and other efforts that enhance oversight of the TiC requirements. By helping states address resource challenges, the grant will strengthen enforcement of these important consumer protections and improve consumers' access to meaningful health care pricing information.

overview.objective: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is offering a cooperative agreement to fund a national technical assistance (TA) entity This entity will support states, U.S. territories, Washington D.C., and small rural hospitals in collecting and reporting financial data related to the cost of maternity, labor, and delivery services. The focus is on small rural hospitals and hospitals where most births are covered by Medicaid or CHIP. The data will help assess service costs, identify factors that affect those costs, and evaluate payments and expected changes in reimbursement. The HHS Secretary will compile state findings into a publicly available report and submit a separate report with recommendations for improving data collection.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: CMS seeks applications for a national, centralized technical assistance (TA) entity to support small rural hospitals and states in providing accurate hospital-based financial data to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) with minimal administrative burden, as well as analysis of that data. Each state, U.S. territory and Washington D.C. will provide data on costs and payments — across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and private insurance – from a representative sample of applicable hospitals, and will conduct analyses including factors impacting cost, expected changes in expenditures and reimbursement, and comparisons of payment rates across types of coverage and payment methods. The TA provider is expected to help identify challenges in providing this information, offer solutions, and provide remedies.

financialInformation.additionalInformation: CMS will make a total of $10,000,000 available to one eligible applicant. Funds will be awarded for 4 years beginning in FY 2027.

TA will also be used to support states in analyses of this data including comparisons of payment sources and methodologies and as analyses of the effects of demographic, geographic, and local economic factors (as defined by the HHS Secretary) on the cost of providing maternity, labor, and delivery services at applicable rural hospitals. Funds may be used to identify challenges hospitals and states have in providing the data, determining how to overcome these challenges and implementing trainings, Q&As, etc. to support accurate data reporting and analysis.

overview.objective: Improve the Quality of Care Provided by Healthcare Systems: Strengthening the overall effectiveness, safety, and patient experience of America’s healthcare systems.
overview.assistanceListingDescription: State and Regional Primary Care Associations (PCAs) provide technical assistance (TA) to existing and potential health centers in their state or region. PCAs support health centers to improve the health of individuals and communities by increasing access to comprehensive, high-quality primary health care; fostering a health center workforce to address current and emerging needs; enhancing emergency preparedness and response; accelerating value-based care delivery; and advancing health center clinical quality and performance. National Technical Assistance Programs (NTAPs) develop, deliver, coordinate, and evaluate national-level TA to existing and potential health centers, both directly and collaboratively with other HRSA-supported TA programs. NTAPs support health centers to deliver comprehensive, high quality primary health care; improve chronic disease management, nutrition and preventive services; improve operational effectiveness, efficiency, and quality; and address emergent public health needs and priorities. Health Center Controlled Networks (HCCNs) support health centers within their established networks by strengthening and leveraging health information technology (HIT) to enhance delivery of affordable, accessible and high-quality primary care, with a focus on data management and analytics, interoperability of systems and digital health tools, and Uniform Data System (UDS) implementation.

awardProcedure.description:
Each application is reviewed against four factors: eligibility, the application deadline, required electronic submission or waiver requested and approved, and the Award Ceiling. If the application does not meet all these factors, then it is disqualified from the merit review process. 
After the initial review, applications are reviewed and evaluated by merit review panels using only the criteria described in the Application Review section of the NOFO. Each panel is composed of experts with knowledge and experience in the area under review. Generally, review panels include three reviewers and one chairperson. 
While merit review scores and their ranking are not binding, ACF does consider them when selecting projects for funding. Scores and rankings are only one element used in the award decision-making process. Other criteria are explained in the Program Description section and in the Application Review section of the NOFO.  ACF reserves the right to evaluate applications in the larger context of the overall portfolio by considering the geographic distribution of federal funds (e.g., ensuring coverage of states, counties, or service areas) in its pre-award decisions. ACF may elect not to fund applicants with management or financial problems that would indicate an inability to successfully complete the proposed project. In addition, ACF may elect to not allow a prime recipient to subaward if there is any indication that they are unable to properly monitor and manage subrecipients. 
Applications may be funded in whole or in part. Successful applicants may be funded at an amount lower than requested.
